justification: No article reports LEMD3 variants in autism probands. The only human variant data is an incidental de novo LEMD3 missense (p.Arg650Cys) found in a schizophrenia trio, predicted benign/tolerated, with no autism phenotype and no replication (PMID 28588275). LEMD3's established disease role is skeletal (osteopoikilosis/Buschke-Ollendorff, BMP/TGF-β signaling; PMIDs 19862465, 35022528), and the gene-trap mouse model shows no neurodevelopmental data. Other co-mentions are purely incidental (autism disclosure tools, parental-care epigenetics, a linkage/CNV survey where LEMD3 is only a neighboring gene). Thus the evidence base is essentially absent, with only weak biological plausibility through nuclear-envelope/BMP signaling warranting partial weight to Hypothesized.

No articles were provided linking ZNF233 to autism spectrum disorder or to any related neurodevelopmental phenotype. Without any literature evidence—genetic, functional, expression-based, or animal model—there is no basis to support an established, existing, or even hypothesized relationship. ZNF233 is a poorly characterized zinc-finger gene with no documented role in neurodevelopment in the supplied evidence set. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with small residual probability assigned to the possibility that unretrieved literature exists.

Two human case reports describe patients carrying de novo SPAST variants who present with autism spectrum disorder in addition to early-onset/complex spastic paraplegia: a mosaic SPAST missense pair in a boy with spastic paraplegia and autism (PMID 28778789, though confounded by a co-occurring 1q21.1 duplication) and two novel de novo missense variants in cis in a 4-year-old with severe ASD and developmental delay (PMID 40870017). A pediatric HSP series also reports autism as a comorbidity in a cohort that includes SPAST patients (PMID 35303589), and SPAST appears in NDD/ASD panel-sequencing cohorts (PMIDs 39457434, 31031587, 31134136, 33970367), although in several of these the variant was of uncertain significance, inherited from an unaffected parent, or part of a multigene CNV (PMID 36750796), which cannot isolate SPAST. Biological plausibility is strong (spastin's role in microtubule severing, neurite outgrowth, ER morphology and dendritic spine formation; PMIDs 29310658, 34927746). Overall this constitutes credible but limited and non-replicated evidence of causation for ASD specifically, best described as Existing rather than Established.

Most of the retrieved articles use "ASD" as a homonym unrelated to autism (atrial septal defect in the congenital heart disease proteomics paper, PMID 37840432; alveolar surface density in the lung fibrosis study, PMID 31600171) and should be dismissed. The Mendelian randomization paper on atopic dermatitis and psychiatric disorders (PMID 38172785) mentions IGLL5 only incidentally within a canine atopic dermatitis gene list, with no human genetic link to autism. The only autism-specific paper (PMID 23275889) lists IGLL5 within a large maternally inherited 22q11.23 multigene gain, which cannot single out IGLL5 from neighboring genes (e.g., BCR, GNAZ) and is explicitly discounted as evidence. No study reports IGLL5-specific variants in independent probands or families, nor any functional/expression data tying IGLL5 biology to autism pathophysiology, so the relationship is best described as Novel with a small allowance for weak hypothesis-generating CNV co-mention.

The strongest human genetic evidence is the large-scale targeted sequencing study (PMID 33004838), which explicitly lists CASZ1 among genes reaching family-wise error rate significance for de novo mutation excess in >17,000 NDD/autism trios — direct variant-level evidence in human probands. Supporting but non-primary evidence includes SFARI "Category 1 (high confidence)" classification of CASZ1 cited in methylation/review papers (PMIDs 42794468, 42401939, 42308296), which are citations of known background rather than independent replication. Other CASZ1 papers concern cardiac development, neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, retinal nuclear organization, or 1p36 contiguous-gene deletions (PMIDs 26345236, 41556146), which cannot isolate CASZ1 from neighbouring genes and therefore do not count toward establishment. Because only one primary study with patient-level variants supports an autism link, without independent replication in a second cohort of probands/families, the evidence best fits "Existing" rather than "Established."

The only available article implicates bi-allelic PRMT9 loss-of-function variants, not TMEM184C, as causal for a neurodevelopmental disorder including autism spectrum disorder. TMEM184C appears solely as an incidental neighboring gene partially included in a copy-number gain in a single family, where the pathogenic mechanism was attributed to PRMT9; a multigenic CNV cannot single out TMEM184C. No functional, expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence linking TMEM184C biology to autism is presented. This is a classic incidental co-mention, supporting the Novel category, with a small residual allowance for the possibility of contributory evidence in the multi-gene CNV.

Multiple human studies report SCN1A variants in independent ASD probands as primary results: O'Roak et al. identified a severe de novo SCN1A mutation in a sporadic ASD trio (21572417); targeted deep sequencing of postmortem ASD brains found recurrent deleterious SCN1A mutations in cases versus controls (26637798); a diverse WES cohort identified a de novo SCN1A frameshift in an ASD proband (39632905); and a Japanese targeted-sequencing case–control study found SCN1A variants associated with ASD/high-functioning autism phenotypes (39280100). In addition, SCN1A-related Dravet syndrome and early SCN1A-related DEE cohorts show high rates of comorbid autistic features (22848613, 36160609, 27653866, 35002916), a well-recognized ASD-linked phenotype. These are human, single-gene (not multigene CNV) findings across several independent cohorts, supporting Established, though some would argue ASD is mainly secondary to the SCN1A epileptic encephalopathy and that early candidate screens were largely negative (12610651), leaving reasonable weight on Existing.

Human genetic evidence exists but is limited: Iossifov et al. (PMID 22542183) report a de novo gene-disrupting (frameshift) mutation in LMTK3 in an ASD proband, and subsequent de novo mutation meta-analyses/candidate prioritizations (PMIDs 33970367, 32066658, 24602502) include LMTK3 among statistically supported or predicted ASD candidate genes, consistent with its SFARI "suggestive evidence" (category 3) classification noted in PMID 42794468. This falls short of Established, since no two independent clinical studies demonstrate replicated, variant-level causal evidence in multiple probands/families; most listings are prioritization or background citations rather than new patient-level findings. Substantial supporting biology comes from non-human work — Lmtk3-KO mice show social, PPI, cognitive and GluA1 trafficking/LTP deficits (PMID 31310731) and LMTK3 regulates KCC2-dependent neuronal excitability (PMID 38715938) — which supports Hypothesized rather than Existing. Overall the weight favors Existing, with meaningful residual probability for Hypothesized if the single de novo event is considered insufficient.

TCF4 haploinsufficiency causes Pitt-Hopkins syndrome, a well-characterized syndromic form of autism, and multiple independent human studies report point/truncating variants in probands with ASD phenotypes. Direct evidence with patient-level variants includes the GALA consortium exome study, where TCF4 reached genome-wide significance as an autism-associated gene with deleterious coding (loss-of-function) variants (PMID 41912808); a 23-patient case series with molecularly confirmed TCF4 variants, many meeting ASD criteria (PMID 29318938); a deep-phenotyping study of 10 PTHS individuals all classified as ASD (PMID 22712893); and de novo TCF4 point mutations identified in ID/ASD diagnostic cohorts (PMIDs 25167861, 25356899, 42427955 – de novo nonsense c.955C>T in an ASD+ID proband). These represent independent probands with single-gene-resolving variants, satisfying replication. Supporting mechanistic work in patient-derived neurons (PMID 37573005) and TCF4 target-gene enrichment for ASD de novo mutations (PMID 29228394) reinforces biological plausibility.

The only article linking RAB17 to autism is a clinical chromosomal microarray study (PMID 37107578), where RAB17 appears merely as one of ~30 genes within a large 2q37.2q37.3 deletion; such a multigene CNV cannot implicate RAB17 specifically (HDAC4 is the recognized driver of 2q37 deletion syndrome), so it does not constitute gene-level evidence. All other papers concern RAB17 biology unrelated to neurodevelopment—epithelial polarized vesicular transport, kidney development, IgA transcytosis, mouse genetic mapping, Rab27A effector screening, and tumour cell migration—with no neuronal or ASD-relevant mechanism. The 17q21.31 variant-to-function study lists RAB17 as a transcriptional target but addresses no autism phenotype, and the mTORC1 review mentions autism only incidentally while not concerning RAB17. There are no human variant-level association or causal data, and no animal/expression model linking RAB17 to autism-relevant biology, so Novel is most probable, with limited weight for Existing based solely on the incidental CNV co-occurrence.

No article reports SEMA4B variants causing ASD in independent probands or families, so Established is excluded. The closest human genetic data is the ASD polygenic risk score study (PMID 32958750), where SEMA4B appears merely as one of many semaphorin/axon-guidance genes within PRS-derived gene sets—suggestive but far from definitive—and a multigenic 15q26 CNV encompassing SEMA4B among ~30 genes in a Chinese ASD cohort (PMID 28670437), which cannot implicate this gene specifically. Other human studies concern schizophrenia-spectrum methylation in 22q11.2DS (PMID 28850114) and a sub-threshold ADHD visuospatial working memory GWAS signal (PMID 37658396), i.e., related but distinct phenotypes. Supporting biological plausibility comes from the maternal inflammation mouse ASD model showing SEMA4B expression changes in microglia (PMID 42493511) and SEMA4B's role in axon guidance/semaphorin–plexin signaling, which is animal/in vitro and therefore Hypothesized. Remaining probability reflects the possibility that all co-mentions are incidental.

Several human studies report point/loss-of-function SETBP1 variants (not just multigene CNVs) in individuals with autism features: the SETBP1-HD/RD cohort of 34 individuals with molecularly confirmed variants reported ASD among the neurodevelopmental impairments (PMID 38923504), the gene-panel study described a de novo missense variant previously reported in an ASD subject plus novel truncating variants (PMID 33391157), and the clinical delineation cohort of 34 LoF/single-gene-deletion carriers documented attention, social and behavioural impairment (PMID 33867525). Comparative phenotyping across rare single-gene variant genotypes found high rates of indicative autism in SETBP1 carriers, though the small sample did not reach significance after correction (PMID 39891993), and SETBP1 is cited as a SFARI Level 1 ASD gene (PMID 41651809). Original CNV/exome morbidity mapping first linked SETBP1 haploinsufficiency to ID and expressive language loss with resequencing in autism cases (PMID 25217958). Evidence is therefore replicated in independent human probands but autism is a variable feature of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome, so points are split between Established and Existing.

AP2S1 emerged from large-scale human exome sequencing of ASD cohorts (Autism Sequencing Consortium) as one of the ~102 de novo mutated risk genes, and it is repeatedly listed among statistically supported ASD genes (PMIDs 32668441, 34768579, 42401939). Human burden analyses report rare loss-of-function variants in AP2S1 conferring an autism odds ratio >8 (PMID 37365347), which is credible human genetic evidence of association. However, within this provided set the primary discovery cohort paper with multiple independent probands is not directly available—most citations restate the association as background—so replicated, proband-level causal demonstration cannot be cited twice. Supporting biology is mainly non-human (zebrafish ap2s1 habituation/behavior-selection work, PMID 38550987) or relates to the unrelated FHH3 calcitropic phenotype (PMIDs 33729479, 28176280), which supports plausibility but not causation of ASD. Hence Existing is the best fit, with meaningful probability for Established.

Human genetic evidence exists: Sanders/Ruzzo-type whole-genome sequencing of multiplex ASD families identified recurrent deletions in the NR3C2 promoter and implicated the gene in ASD risk (PMID 31398340), and a separate family study reported a maternally inherited stop-gain variant (p.Q919X) shared by three affected brothers (PMID 32064789). Additional WGS work cites NR3C2 among genes with recurrent disruptive de novo events and regulatory disruption (PMID 26749308), but that statement is largely background rather than its own primary finding. Supporting functional data (zebrafish nr3c2 loss causing sleep and social deficits) are non-human and therefore bolster a hypothesized/mechanistic rather than causal human claim. Because the clearly gene-specific coding evidence rests essentially on a single family, with the other support coming from non-coding structural variants and citations, the evidence is credible but not definitively replicated across independent probands, favoring "Existing" over "Established".

Large de novo variant analyses in human trios implicate PBX1 as a neurodevelopmental disorder gene, with DNMs observed across ASD/DD/ID cohorts (PMID 36350923; PMID 33970367), though PBX1 reached exome-wide significance only when ASD and DD cohorts were combined, and no ASD-specific signal was claimed. Clinical PBX1 haploinsufficiency (CAKUTHED) consistently includes developmental delay and intellectual disability, ASD-adjacent phenotypes, and a minimally verbal autistic patient carried a PBX1 nonsense variant, albeit alongside a pathogenic TBR1 variant (PMIDs 34797033, 33098248, 41716258). Functional human iPSC work shows PBX1 is a convergent downstream node of three autism risk genes regulating neural progenitor proliferation (PMID 40161581), which supports biological plausibility but does not involve PBX1 variants in patients. Because no two independent primary studies demonstrate PBX1 point variants causing ASD in distinct probands (deletion/CNV reports cannot isolate the gene), "Established" is not justified; the human de novo variant evidence supports "Existing," with remaining weight on "Hypothesized" given the mechanistic/convergence data.

Multiple independent human studies report point/loss-of-function variants in SATB2 in probands with autism or autism-related neurodevelopmental phenotypes: the GALA consortium sequencing study (PMID 41912808) lists SATB2 among genome-wide significant autism-associated genes (p < 1e-18) based on deleterious coding variants; a WES study of CNV-negative ASD children identified a causative SATB2 loss-of-function variant (PMID 40642607); and the Brazilian ASD exome cohort reported a de novo SATB2 stopgain in an ASD proband (PMID 42721435). Deep-phenotyping cohorts of molecularly confirmed SATB2-associated syndrome document autism diagnoses in 41% of adolescents/adults (PMID 33969926) and a distinctive autistic behavioural phenotype in 81 individuals (PMID 35350986), supporting a causal gene-level relationship rather than a contiguous-gene effect. Earlier work establishing SATB2 as a single-gene contributor disrupted by balanced chromosomal abnormalities in autism/NDD cases (PMID 22521361) and the original nonsense mutation report (PMID 17377962) further support causality, so Established is most likely, with residual probability on Existing given that most abstracts restate the association rather than demonstrate it anew.

The only human genetic evidence linking SLC4A9 to ASD is the de novo mutation/TADA analysis (PMID 32066658), where SLC4A9 appears among prioritized candidate genes at a permissive threshold (0.05 < FDR < 0.1) in a male-specific subgroup; this is a single, statistically suggestive report rather than replicated clinical confirmation, which fits "Existing" at best and certainly not "Established" (no two independent proband/family reports of causal variants exist). All remaining SLC4A9 literature concerns renal intercalated cell transcription, salivary/enamel physiology, and anion/bicarbonate transport mechanisms (PMIDs 42855468, 38536494, 36603001, 19544066, 16159312, 40327716, 12847417), with no ASD relevance. One pH-regulation review mentions AE4/SLC4A9 only in passing while discussing NHE6/NHE9 in autism (PMID 26965387), a co-mention rather than evidence, and the microglia review ties SLC4A9 to depression risk loci, not ASD (PMID 42244505). Some probability remains for "Novel" given the weak, borderline-significance nature of the single ASD finding, and for "Hypothesized" given generic pH-homeostasis relevance to neuronal excitability.

No article reports PDE4C variants in autism patients; there are no probands or families with PDE4C mutations linked to ASD, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded. The human paternal-age methylation study (PMID 28171595) included PDE4C only as a candidate gene for neuropsychiatric risk and found no significant age-related methylation change, which is a co-mention rather than association evidence. Supportive but indirect biological rationale comes from the cAMP/PDE4 pathway literature in fragile X and autism (PMID 18601949, 38860393), DISC1/PDE4 synaptic and social-behavior rescue in mice/iPSCs (PMID 33658519), and downregulation of Pde4c in cerebella of mouse offspring in a gestational folate model that also altered ASD-associated genes (PMID 25629700). Other papers are purely enzymological, renal (PMID 21670265), immunological, or canine muscle phenotypes (PMID 38473107) and provide no ASD link, so a substantial share of probability remains on Novel.

Human genetic evidence for intragenic CTCF variants in neurodevelopmental disorders with autistic features comes from several independent sources: the large-scale targeted sequencing study reporting de novo CTCF mutation enrichment in NDD/autism trios with explicit genotype–phenotype correlation for CTCF (PMID 33004838), a cohort of four unrelated Chinese probands with distinct de novo CTCF point/frameshift/intragenic variants presenting developmental delay and autistic-like behavior (PMID 42792888), a clinical ASD cohort reporting a de novo probably pathogenic CTCF missense variant (PMID 38587680), and the clinical synopsis of CTCF-related disorder (PMID 38662876). These are independent probands with single-gene-resolution variants, supporting an Established causal role, though the core phenotype is ID/NDD with autistic features rather than idiopathic ASD, which keeps meaningful weight on Existing. Mouse conditional knockout studies (PMIDs 29133437, 35379308, 30377227) and chromatin/CTCF-binding-site studies in ASD regulatory genomics (PMIDs 38280381, 42281968) provide supportive mechanistic biology but are non-human or indirect.

Multiple independent human probands with de novo missense CACNA1D variants and ASD are reported with primary genetic data: Pinggera et al. (PMID 25620733) describe de novo p.A749G and p.G407R in two unrelated ASD/ID probands; a third de novo variant p.V401L was identified in a patient with ASD and epilepsy (PMID 28472301); a novel de novo p.G1169D was found in children with ASD-spectrum neurodevelopmental disease (PMID 39246741); and an inherited gain-of-function p.S672L segregated with ASD/ID in a family (PMID 37122292). Large-scale exome sequencing in the GALA consortium independently identified CACNA1D as a genome-wide significant autism-associated gene (PMID 41912808), and functional/electrophysiological work (PMIDs 30465465, 38553610, 27255217) plus a knock-in mouse model (PMID 37698939) supports a gain-of-function mechanism. Together these constitute replicated, single-gene-resolved human evidence, supporting "Established"; a small residual probability for "Existing" reflects that many variants are missense of variable penetrance and the ASD phenotype is part of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome.

The strongest mechanistic data are from mouse models: Sarm1 knockdown and PV-neuron-specific Sarm1 conditional knockout mice show social interaction deficits, repetitive behaviors, altered synaptic plasticity and rescue by an mGluR5 PAM (PMIDs 35869039, 24321214, 24744698), which alone would support only "Hypothesized." However, there is limited human genetic evidence: SARM1 appears among prioritized ASD candidate genes derived from de novo mutation burden/TADA analyses (PMID 32066658) and as a top discriminating gene in exome-trio machine-learning analysis of ASD versus schizophrenia (PMID 32111185), with a (non-validated) de novo missense variant also noted in an ADHD sequencing study (PMID 28332277). These are suggestive but not replicated in independent probands with clear causal demonstration, so "Established" is not warranted — no two articles report patient-level variants with independent replication for ASD. Most remaining papers concern SARM1's axon-degeneration/NADase biology and are unrelated to ASD genetics, and several ASD mentions are background citations rather than new evidence.

Human large-scale de novo mutation studies list VEZF1 among genes with an excess of damaging DNMs in autism/developmental delay cohorts (PMID 30559488; PMID 33970367), and it appears among the "novel" ASD/NDD genes from the Autism Sequencing Consortium 102-gene list discussed in subsequent reviews (PMID 34768579; PMID 32668441; PMID 42401939). These are credible human genetic signals from probands with de novo variants, but the evidence is statistical and largely from overlapping mega-cohorts, with few detailed independent probands or families and limited genotype–phenotype characterization, so replication required for "Established" is not clearly demonstrated. Supporting biology (VEZF1 regulates DNMT3b-dependent genomic DNA methylation, brain microvascular development, and is implicated in prenatal alcohol exposure/FASD models) provides plausible neurodevelopmental mechanism but is non-human/in vitro (PMIDs 18676812, 36109176, 41668336), so it backs "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing." Overall, "Existing" is the best fit.

Human genetic evidence exists but is limited: a large de novo variant meta-analysis listed LRRC4 among new ASD candidate genes with recurrent de novo coding variants (PMID 31332282), and MPRA screens identified patient-derived 5'UTR de novo mutations in LRRC4 altering translation in neurons (PMIDs 37961498, 41344325). Other human reports are multigene CNVs (7q31.33q32.1 microdeletion with GRM8, PMID 28224041; duplication in a Taiwanese ASD cohort, PMID 28931914), which cannot isolate LRRC4 from neighboring genes and therefore do not establish causality. Strong supporting biology comes from animal work: Lrrc4/NGL-2 knockout mice show autistic-like behaviors rescued by NMDAR activation (PMID 29949768), and its trans-synaptic partner NTNG2 is implicated in human autistic features (PMID 31372774). Overall this supports "Existing" (credible but non-definitive human association) with residual weight on "Hypothesized" since much of the mechanistic support is murine/in vitro.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo coding variants in EBF3 (frameshift, nonsense, splice, missense) in probands with hypotonia, developmental delay, intellectual disability and autism: PMID 29162653 described seven unrelated individuals with de novo EBF3 variants including autism, and PMID 34256850 identified both coding and noncoding (enhancer hs737) de novo variants in simplex autism cohorts with EBF3 reaching genome-wide significance for DNVs in NDD. PMID 35340043 provides a large independent cohort (83 individuals) with genotype–phenotype correlation in EBF3-related autism spectrum/neurodevelopmental disorder, and PMIDs 28017370/28017373 report further independent de novo point variants in neurodevelopmental syndrome patients. These are point/intragenic variants in humans, not solely multigenic CNVs, satisfying replication across independent probands; EBF3 is also an SFARI category 1 (high confidence) ASD gene. Residual probability is given to "Existing" because autism is a variable rather than invariant feature of the EBF3-related syndrome (HADDS), with ataxia/ID being the core phenotype.

PMID 33658631 reports its own cohort of individuals (15 with RFX3 variants, mostly de novo frameshift, splice-site, and missense changes) presenting ASD, intellectual disability, and ADHD, providing multi-proband human genetic evidence that singles out RFX3. Independent case reports add replication: PMID 40200712 documents RFX3 haploinsufficiency identified by long-read genome sequencing in an adolescent with autism and intellectual disability, and PMID 37717291 describes a patient with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome and ASD carrying an RFX3 mutation (with PMID 42653242 reporting a second IESS case via a 9p24.2 deletion involving RFX3, which is supportive though CNV-based). Functional human stem cell/organoid work (PMIDs 40060598, 38827400, 40552535) mechanistically corroborates that RFX3 loss-of-function disrupts neuronal differentiation, synaptic and activity-dependent gene programs, and ciliogenesis, and RFX3 is a SFARI category 1 gene. Together these constitute replicated human variant-level evidence plus mechanism, supporting an Established classification, with residual probability on Existing given the modest number of fully independent SNV-level probands outside the original cohort.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report de novo point/truncating variants in DYRK1A in ASD probands with primary data: O'Roak et al. found recurrent de novo disruptive mutations in 2446 ASD probands (PMID 23160955); a large resequencing of 7162 ASD/DD patients showed significant enrichment and excess of de novo truncating DYRK1A mutations defining a syndromic ASD/ID phenotype (PMID 25707398); ten unrelated patients with nonsense/frameshift/missense DYRK1A variants presenting with autism and microcephaly (PMID 25920557); two further unrelated patients with de novo nonsense and missense variants (PMID 25641759); and five DYRK1A variants identified in ASD patients with functional follow-up (PMID 28167836). Standardized phenotyping cohorts confirm ASD as a core feature of DYRK1A haploinsufficiency syndrome (PMIDs 35285131, 38622540). Animal/zebrafish and iPSC work (PMIDs 29021890, 38382213, 40050271) provide supportive mechanism but are not needed given the replicated human single-gene variant evidence. This clearly meets the Established threshold with multiple independent probands carrying gene-specific (non-CNV) variants.

Several human studies report de novo point/frameshift variants in SYNCRIP in independent probands with neurodevelopmental phenotypes that include autism: the genome-sequencing ASD cohort reported two de novo missense variants in SYNCRIP in autism patients (PMID 30504930), a case series described three additional individuals with novel de novo SYNCRIP variants with ID and autistic features (PMID 34157790), the hnRNP gene-family study found SYNCRIP significantly enriched for de novo variants with phenotypic characterization (PMID 33874999), and the large trio meta-analyses identified SYNCRIP as exome-wide significant for NDD including ASD probands (PMID 27479843, PMID 36350923). These are single-gene variants in humans across independent cohorts, supporting a causal SYNCRIP-related NDD with frequent ASD, which pushes toward Established. However, much of the strongest statistical evidence is for broad NDD/ID rather than ASD specifically (one analysis explicitly found no ASD-specific signal), and some supporting reports are multigenic 6q deletions (PMID 29904178, PMID 26185640) that cannot isolate SYNCRIP, so substantial weight remains on Existing.

Two independent clinical reports provide primary human evidence of causation: PMID 39721588 describes 29 individuals with heterozygous UBR5 variants presenting with a neurodevelopmental syndrome including autism, supported by functional ubiquitination and C. elegans data, and PMID 41318701 reports three additional unrelated probands with de novo loss-of-function variants and ASD/ID, reviewing 11 de novo LoF variants in total. Independent sequencing studies add further de novo single-nucleotide/frameshift events in ASD probands (PMID 38519481, PMID 31413120), and UBR5 emerges in large rare-variant ASD gene discovery efforts (PMID 35982160). These are human, single-gene–resolving variants in multiple independent probands, satisfying criteria for Established. Remaining probability reflects residual uncertainty about whether autism is a consistent core feature versus part of a broader neurodevelopmental phenotype.

Primary human genetic evidence with SMARCC2-specific variants in ASD probands comes from independent cohorts: the ASD genome sequencing study reporting a de novo loss-of-function SMARCC2 variant returned as a clinically relevant ASD finding (PMID 40169255), the Brazilian ASD exome cohort reporting a de novo stopgain in an ASD proband (PMID 42721435), a de novo intragenic inversion disrupting SMARCC2 in a patient with ASD/OCD/ADHD (PMID 41291750), and a case-control burden analysis showing enrichment of rare missense/frameshift BAF-gene variants including SMARCC2 in Japanese ASD patients (PMID 35699097). Large SMARCC2-NDD cohorts (PMIDs 37551667, 30580808, 41532374) consistently describe behavioral/autistic features with de novo variants, supporting a syndromic ASD phenotype. Mechanistic work in mice and human iPSC neurons (PMID 42649243) adds biological plausibility but is supportive rather than the basis of the human link. Because at least two independent single-gene, patient-level reports exist, Established is favored, though some weight remains on Existing since several reports are small case series or VUS-level findings.

Most of the supplied articles concern genes that merely share the "SET" string (SETBP1, SETD1B, SETD2, SETD5) or use "set" as an ordinary English word (e.g., "gene set", "fire set", "significance level was set"), and must be dismissed as homonyms. The only item genuinely about the SET gene (PMID 35122673) describes a 2.0 Mb 9q34.11 deletion encompassing SET and SPTAN1 in a single male with nonsyndromic intellectual disability and mild dysmorphism; a multigene deletion cannot isolate SET, and autism is not the reported phenotype, so this does not establish causation for ASD. It does, however, place SET within a neurodevelopmental/intellectual-disability spectrum that overlaps ASD risk, giving some weight to "Existing"/"Hypothesized". No point-variant studies in ASD probands, no functional or model data linking SET specifically to autistic phenotypes are present in this corpus, so "Established" is untenable and a substantial probability remains for "Novel".

No article reports ADAM21 variants causing autism in independent probands; the only human ASD study (PMID 35762097) lists ADAM21 merely as one gene among many within multigene CNVs and in gene-ontology enrichment output, which cannot single out ADAM21 and thus does not constitute evidence of causation. The motor coordination GWAS (PMID 34177493) reports only suggestive, non-genome-wide-significant SNPs near ADAM20/ADAM21 for developmental coordination disorder, a neurodevelopmental trait related to but distinct from ASD — this provides at best weak human associative support. The ADAM family review (PMID 31236626) establishes ADAM21 biology in neuronal regeneration/nervous system, supporting a plausible but indirect biological rationale, i.e., a hypothesized link. Given the incidental nature of the ASD co-mention, substantial probability also remains for Novel, with Established essentially excluded.

Direct human evidence exists: a de novo CAMK2A E183V variant was identified in an ASD proband and functionally validated (PMID 28130356), and a clinical WES cohort of 288 Saudi children with DSM-5 ASD listed CAMK2A among recurrently affected genes with pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants (PMID 42606785). Additional large de novo variant series (PMIDs 29100089, 29560374, 37510258) establish CAMK2A as a monogenic neurodevelopmental disorder gene (IDD53) whose phenotypic spectrum explicitly includes autism spectrum behaviors, supporting a strongly linked precursor/overlapping phenotype. However, most of these studies ascertain for intellectual disability/epilepsy rather than ASD per se, and the only clearly ASD-ascertained proband-level report is a single case, so replication specifically for ASD is thin; common-variant work (PMID 29147782) is only nominally significant. Mouse knock-in and organoid/expression studies add mechanistic support but are non-human. On balance, the evidence best fits Existing with substantial probability of Established.

Two large human sequencing studies report their own variant-level findings implicating PHF12: Coe et al. (PMID 30559488) identified PHF12 among genes with an excess of de novo mutations across 10,927 developmental delay/autism probands, and Wang et al. (PMID 33004838) found 6 ultra-rare LGD mutations in 16,321 NDD cases plus de novo enrichment reaching family-wise error significance, with PHF12 listed among genes newly attaining FWER significance. These are human, variant-based data, but the cohorts are mixed neurodevelopmental (DD/ID/ASD) rather than ASD-specific, and the two datasets partially overlap, limiting true independent replication for the autism phenotype specifically. Supporting but non-decisive mentions include PHF12 being cited as a high-confidence autism gene in the ASD-megalencephaly network analysis (PMID 39887636) and ASD gene lists (PMID 42401939); CNV-based reports at 17q11.2 (PMIDs 27247625, 38850022, 37686052) span many genes and cannot isolate PHF12. Therefore Existing is most probable, with substantial residual probability for Established.

No articles were provided, so there is no literature evidence linking KLK4 variants or biology to congenital heart disease. KLK4 (kallikrein-related peptidase 4) is primarily known for its role in enamel maturation (amelogenesis imperfecta) and prostate/tumor biology, with no recognized cardiac developmental function. Without any human genetic studies, functional data, or animal models connecting the gene to cardiac malformation, neither Established nor Existing can be supported. A small residual probability is retained for Hypothesized given the general plausibility of protease involvement in developmental processes, but the relationship is best described as Novel.

The only primary patient-based study in the list is PMID 35916866, which reports 11 unrelated individuals with (mostly de novo) ZMYND8 variants causing a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability and cardiac anomalies — directly relevant to ASD-related neurodevelopment but not framed as an ASD cohort. Several reviews (PMIDs 31220745, 34768579, 42401939, 42794468) list ZMYND8 as an ASD risk gene based on the Autism Sequencing Consortium exome study (Satterstrom et al.) and SFARI Category 1 classification, but these are secondary citations rather than independent primary evidence. The remaining papers (PMIDs 26655721, 34764296, 36153585) are purely molecular/chromatin-biology studies, and PMID 36803626 is a rat BPA model, supporting only biological plausibility. Since I cannot cite two independent primary human studies with ZMYND8 variants in ASD probands, Established is not justified, and Existing best captures the credible but limited/indirect human genetic evidence.

No article in this set reports POLE3 variants in autism patients or any genetic association with ASD; the POLE3 literature concerns DNA polymerase epsilon function, replication stress, DNA repair, lymphocyte development, tumorigenesis and mutational biases (PMIDs 31506018, 32553171, 37682991, 29754823, 34947512, 40806440). The autism articles are entirely unrelated, concerning Cntnap2, Shank3, RBM8A, GABAergic/serotonergic development, valproic acid models and caregiver experiences, with no mention of POLE3. The only tenuous biological bridge is the finding that Pole3 deletion in mouse embryonic stem cells disrupts symmetric parental histone inheritance and impairs neural differentiation and development (PMID 37666989), plus general reports that Polε destabilization causes developmental abnormalities (PMID 29754823), which could conceivably be relevant to neurodevelopment but is not autism-specific. Therefore the co-mentions are essentially incidental, and the relationship is best described as Novel, with a modest allowance for a hypothesized neurodevelopmental mechanism.

Several large human de novo variant studies implicate PAPOLG at gene level in ASD/NDD: Coe et al. (PMID 30559488) report an excess of severe missense de novo mutations in PAPOLG and nominate it as a second candidate within the 2p15-p16.1 critical region; the MSSNG whole-genome study (PMID 36368308) identifies PAPOLG as a TADA+ ASD gene driven by de novo damaging missense variants; and the integrated 46,612-trio analysis (PMID 36350923) finds PAPOLG significant in ASD trios with additional DD de novo variants. These are human, variant-level data, supporting more than a hypothesis, but they are statistical gene-discovery results from partially overlapping cohorts without detailed independent clinical proband reports or functional validation, so replication is not definitive. The remaining literature consists of multigene 2p15p16.1 deletions/duplications (PMIDs 28573701, 23495096, 24810580, 36807877, 28717667), which cannot isolate PAPOLG from neighbours such as BCL11A, REL, USP34, and indeed point to those genes as the main drivers. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with modest weight to Established and Hypothesized.

Human genetic evidence from independent cohorts supports a causal role: PMID 27824329 reported recurrent de novo likely gene-disrupting mutations in WDFY3 among 1,543 Chinese ASD probands, and PMID 30564305 (ACGC phase II) independently replicated disruptive WDFY3 mutations associated with ASD/macrocephaly. PMID 31327001 described 13 probands with mostly de novo, protein-truncating or missense WDFY3 variants causing neurodevelopmental delay with autism/ADHD, and PMID 42800802 expanded this to a 32-patient LoF cohort with autism and ADHD features. These are single-nucleotide/indel level variants in multiple unrelated probands, not multigene CNVs, meeting the replication requirement. Extensive supporting mouse and Drosophila work (PMIDs 25198012, 35733184, 32609087) provides mechanistic plausibility (neurogenesis, migration, synaptic plasticity), but the human data alone are decisive. Some residual probability is assigned to Existing because the core phenotype is often broader neurodevelopmental delay with ASD as a frequent comorbidity rather than isolated ASD.

Sands et al. (PMID 31177578) report 11 independent patients with recurrent de novo KCNQ3 missense variants (R230C/H/S, R227Q), all with autistic features and formal ASD diagnosis in 5/11, with patch-clamp confirmation of gain-of-function — this is primary causal evidence in humans. Gamba et al./Gilling et al. (PMID 23596459) independently identified a de novo translocation truncating KCNQ3 in a boy with childhood autism plus three unrelated autistic individuals carrying p.P574S with functional consequences. Further independent probands and families with single-gene KCNQ3 variants and ASD phenotypes are documented (PMIDs 32580997, 35384780, 42255468, 42024975), and large-scale targeted sequencing established KCNQ3 as a significant NDD/ASD risk gene with genotype–phenotype correlation (PMID 33004838). These are point/truncating variants in a single gene, not multigene CNVs, and are replicated across independent cohorts, supporting the Established category; some residual probability is retained for Existing since the dominant phenotype is often epilepsy/DEE with ASD as a comorbid feature.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo single-nucleotide/indel STXBP1 variants in probands carrying an ASD diagnosis: a Chinese ASD cohort sequencing study identified de novo mutations in STXBP1 among ASD risk genes (PMID 27824329); whole-exome sequencing diagnosed a de novo c.874C>T (p.Arg292Cys) in a boy with ASD (PMID 34840252); a novel splice variant (c.38-2A>G) was found in a child with ID, epilepsy and autism (PMID 39359953); an Indian ASD diagnostic-yield study found a likely pathogenic c.874C>A in an ASD patient (PMID 40117183); and a Brazilian ASD exome cohort reported a de novo c.874C>T in a proband (PMID 42721435). These are independent probands with gene-level resolution (not multigene CNVs), supporting a causal/contributory role, and STXBP1 is a SFARI category-1 ASD gene. Counterweighing a full Established call, large sequencing studies note that ASD is comparatively rare among STXBP1 carriers and often appears as a comorbid feature of the dominant DEE phenotype (PMIDs 29264391, 26865513), which keeps substantial probability on "Existing." Animal (Stxbp1+/-) and organoid data (PMIDs 29040524, 41741416) add mechanistic support but do not themselves establish human causality.

Human evidence directly linking GABRA1 variants to ASD exists but is limited: PMID 37434477 describes a single patient with a de novo loss-of-function GABRA1 variant (p.Arg112Gln) presenting with autism spectrum disorder plus refractory epilepsy, and PMID 38256266 reports de novo/qualifying GABRA1 variants in ASD probands from trio whole-genome sequencing (though classified as a second-tier, not primary, ASD gene). Reviews (PMIDs 41625255, 35718920) note GABRA1 de novo missense variants in patients with ASD co-occurring with epilepsy/ID, but these largely restate the association as background rather than provide new primary proband data. Candidate-gene association studies that explicitly tested GABRA1 SNPs were negative for GABRA1 itself (PMIDs 16080114, 24249596), with signals attributed to GABRA4/GABRB3/GABRD. GABRA1 is, however, firmly established in epileptic encephalopathy/Dravet-spectrum neurodevelopmental disorders (PMIDs 24623842, 23934111, 31618474), phenotypes strongly linked to ASD, supporting "Existing" rather than "Established", since independent, well-powered ASD-specific proband replication isolating GABRA1 is not yet demonstrated.

SEC23A is firmly established as the gene for cranio-lenticulo-sutural dysplasia (CLSD), a craniofacial/skeletal/lens disorder, but almost none of the listed literature addresses cardiac malformations. The only direct human link is PMID 37828500, in which a proband with novel compound heterozygous SEC23A variants (both classified as VUS) is described as having "skeletal, cardiac, ocular, and hearing defects" — a single, non-replicated proband with an incidentally noted cardiac phenotype, which at best supports "Existing" and certainly not "Established." The remaining papers (PMIDs 16980979, 17981132, 21039434, 34580982, 38275611, 27148587, 22298774) concern COPII-mediated collagen/procollagen secretion, craniofacial dysmorphism, cataract and skeletal disease, while the zebrafish crusher model (PMID 16980978) shows craniofacial chondrocyte defects without reported heart malformation. Because the sole cardiac mention is a single phenotypic descriptor rather than a dedicated genetic association study, substantial probability also remains for "Novel" or merely mechanism-based "Hypothesized" (ER-to-Golgi secretion of extracellular matrix proteins is plausibly relevant to cardiac development).

All retrieved literature on RHOBTB2 concerns neurodevelopmental phenotypes: developmental and epileptic encephalopathy type 64, alternating hemiplegia of childhood, paroxysmal movement disorders, dystonia, and Rett-like presentations, plus a tumor-suppressor role in cancer. No article reports cardiac malformations, structural heart defects, or any congenital heart disease phenotype in patients with RHOBTB2 variants. Reported extra-neurological features (skin color change, gastrointestinal symptoms, peripheral vasomotor disturbance) are autonomic/paroxysmal and not cardiac structural defects. There is also no expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence linking RHOBTB2 to cardiac development in these abstracts (Drosophila work addresses neuronal/dendritic function). Therefore the gene–phenotype relationship with congenital heart disease is best classified as Novel.

IRF2BPL is firmly established as a cause of a human neurodevelopmental disorder (NEDAMSS) with regression, epilepsy, loss of speech and movement abnormalities (PMID 30057031, 39843638, 38481258), a phenotype spectrum in which autistic features are repeatedly reported, making it at minimum a strongly linked neurodevelopmental mechanism/precursor for ASD. Direct ASD-specific evidence exists but is thin: a trio-WES cohort of NDD with comorbid ASD reports one proband with a pathogenic IRF2BPL variant classified among high-confidence/syndromic ASD genes (PMID 38764027), and a Simons Searchlight somatic-variant study includes an IRF2BPL proband in an ASD-enriched cohort (PMID 40182320); IRF2BPL also appears in de novo mutation gene lists for ASD, but only as background/compiled data (PMID 30298087, 42401939, 42526765). I cannot cite two independent primary studies whose own results report multiple ASD probands specifically attributable to IRF2BPL, so "Established" is not warranted. Remaining weight goes to Hypothesized, reflecting supportive functional/model-organism work (Drosophila pits, zebrafish irf2bpl) and WNT/transcriptional regulation biology relevant to neurodevelopment.

Multiple human studies report intragenic, sequence-level EHMT1 variants (not just multigene deletions) in independent probands with autistic phenotypes: a de novo nonsense variant (p.Trp1138Ter) in an autistic patient with Kleefstra syndrome (PMID 27651234), a de novo splice-site variant (c.2750-1G>T) in a patient with an early autism diagnosis (PMID 28361099), and a large clinical cohort of 65 Kleefstra patients in which 54% carried sequence variants and 38% met criteria for autism spectrum disorder (PMID 39746677). Additional human series report de novo EHMT1 point/splice variants in patients with neurodevelopmental disease including ASD (PMIDs 33834462, 31171384, 29069077), and balanced chromosomal abnormality sequencing directly disrupted EHMT1 in autism/NDD cases (PMID 22521361). Candidate resequencing in Japanese ASD subjects found rare EHMT1 missense variants but without statistical significance (PMID 25400900), and supportive mechanistic work exists in mouse and iPSC models (PMIDs 29554304, 31914384, 28742076), which reinforces but does not alone prove causality. The convergence of replicated human probands with intragenic variants and ASD features supports an Established relationship, with residual probability on Existing because much of the autism evidence is embedded within the broader syndromic Kleefstra phenotype.

The bulk of the ADCY5 literature here concerns ADCY5-related hyperkinetic movement disorders (chorea, dyskinesia, myoclonus-dystonia), with no autism causality demonstrated, so Established is essentially excluded. Two human studies provide weak, candidate-level support: a deep exome study of ASD brains reporting a low-level brain somatic ADCY5 missense variant in an ASD proband (PMID 39085355), and an ASD-with-disproportionate-megalencephaly cohort listing ADCY5 among genes with de novo protein-impacting variants (PMID 39887636); these are discovery lists rather than replicated causal evidence, supporting "Existing" at most. Strong biological plausibility comes from non-human data: Adcy5-knockout mice show autism-like social deficits and repetitive grooming, reversed by probiotic-derived EVs (PMID 40164687), plus striatal cAMP/D2-receptor signaling relevance and ADCY5 expression findings in an ASD mouse model (PMID 41920999), which support Hypothesized. Some mentions (e.g., PMID 41039503 citing ADCY5 for gestational duration) are incidental, leaving a small probability for Novel.

Human genetic evidence firmly establishes that de novo and inherited TAOK1 variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMIDs 31230721, 33565190, 35091509, 39737487), and the NDD phenotype explicitly includes behavioral abnormalities, autism or autistic traits, and macrocephaly — a well-recognized ASD subtype. Direct ASD-specific proband evidence is thinner: PMID 37656623 reports a de novo frameshift TAOK1 variant identified in a Chinese ASD cohort, but the bulk of that study's causal demonstration is a mouse haploinsufficiency model, and the large cohort paper (PMID 39737487) assigns autism chiefly to TAOK2 while describing TAOK1 mainly as NDD with variable behavioral features. Thus only one clearly ASD-ascertained human proband series exists, falling short of the two independent patient-based ASD studies required for "Established." Mechanistic work in neurons (PMIDs 36595571, 37230852) supports biological plausibility but is non-human/in vitro. Accordingly, "Existing" is the most likely category, with meaningful probability for "Established" given the breadth of pathogenic single-gene human variants with autistic phenotypes.

Most of the retrieved articles concern ATP2B2 (a paralog on 3p25.3), not ATP2B4, and those association/GWAS/family studies cannot be credited to ATP2B4. Several ATP2B4 papers are irrelevant to autism (malaria susceptibility, cardiac remodeling/PMCA4 rodent work, hyperaldosteronism, developmental dysplasia of the hip). Direct human ATP2B4–ASD data are limited to a single family pedigree WES study in which two affected siblings shared a rare missense variant (ATP2B4 c.G1996A/p.A666T), which the authors did not nominate as a credible ASD gene (PMID 34368859), and a haplotype-resolved methylome study where ATP2B4 carried recurrent methylation outliers in a few ASD probands (PMID 42308296) — neither is replicated causal evidence. Biological plausibility is reasonable (PMCA4 mediates Ca2+ efflux, and calcium-signaling dysregulation plus the closely related ATP2B2 are implicated in ASD), supporting a Hypothesized-to-Existing rating; Established is excluded as no two independent probands/families with convincing causal variants are reported.

H1-4 (HIST1H1E) frameshift variants cause Rahman syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism spectrum disorder/behavioral problems are a recurrent feature. Primary patient-level evidence includes PMID 29704315 (de novo c.435dupC in a boy with autism and intellectual disability, with functional demonstration of haploinsufficiency), PMID 34788807 (newly identified C- and N-terminal H1-4 variants in patients with RMNS, which includes ASD, plus neuronal functional characterization), PMID 37605493 (novel de novo frameshift proband plus curation of 52 patients where autism/behavior problems are common), and PMID 31400068 (30 individuals with HIST1H1E PTVs with ID and behavioral issues). Large-scale rare variant studies (PMID 35982160) also list HIST1H1E among ASD/DD-associated genes, supporting independent replication of single-gene (not CNV-based) causation. Points are withheld from full certainty because ASD is a variable component of a broader syndromic phenotype rather than the primary discrete diagnosis in most reports.

No article reports NUDCD2 variants causing autism in independent probands; the only clinical variant paper (PMID 37272762) describes biallelic loss-of-function causing a multiple malformation syndrome with cholestasis, renal failure and early death, not ASD, so Established is excluded. Human genetic support comes indirectly from PMID 32066658, where NUDCD2 was prioritized as an ASD candidate gene from de novo mutation/TADA analysis in patient cohorts, and from network meta-analyses of ASD-associated genes (PMIDs 31323926, 38102483) that include NUDCD2 — these constitute limited, non-definitive human association evidence consistent with "Existing." Supporting biology is plausible but non-human/in vitro: NudCL2 regulates LIS1 and myosin-9 stability in cell migration and acts as an autophagy receptor promoting ciliogenesis (PMIDs 32665550, 34480124), and it was identified as a HERC2 interactor, a gene linked to Angelman syndrome and ASD (PMID 25476789), supporting a Hypothesized weighting. Because the candidate-gene listings are derived from large prioritization pipelines rather than replicated, variant-level clinical findings, a meaningful probability remains for Novel.

Multiple human studies report de novo point variants in SOX11 (missense/nonsense) in patients with a neurodevelopmental syndrome (IDDMOH / Coffin-Siris-like), and autism/autistic features are explicitly part of the phenotype: PMID 39333428 describes seven new patients with de novo SOX11 variants of whom 5/7 had autism/ADHD, PMID 37916390 documents autistic-feature subscale impairment in verbal individuals with SOX11 syndrome, and PMID 33921431 identified a de novo SOX11 missense variant in an ASD diagnostic WES cohort. PMID 33970367 further prioritized SOX11 as a cross-disorder de novo mutation candidate gene including ASD cases, and PMID 34205270 notes SOX-related BAF variants are most associated with neurodevelopmental/behavioral differences. These are human, point-variant based and from independent cohorts, supporting a causal link, though ASD here is a feature of a broader syndromic ID phenotype rather than isolated autism, and the deletion-based report (PMID 18992374) cannot single out SOX11. Supporting mechanistic/animal data (PMID 34184026, 24886874, 40950130) is consistent but secondary.

The only direct human evidence linking NALCN to congenital heart disease is the integrative CNV/DNV burden analysis (PMID 34324492), which flags NALCN as a novel candidate haploinsufficient CHD gene, and a review noting NALCN among genes within rare CNVs in tetralogy of Fallot cohorts (PMID 23934094); both rest largely on multigene copy number changes and therefore cannot single out NALCN, precluding "Established". The PAGE prenatal exome study reported a de novo NALCN missense variant in a fetus with multisystem anomalies, but not specifically attributed to a cardiac phenotype (PMID 30712880). The remainder of the literature concerns NALCN channelopathy syndromes (CLIFAHDD, IHPRF1) and UNC79/UNC80 disorders, which are neurodevelopmental with no consistent CHD component (PMIDs 29168298, 37452996, 40048676, 27844033, 29610177). Thus a limited, non-definitive human association exists, best described as "Existing", with meaningful residual probability that the co-mentions are incidental (Novel) or purely candidate/biological (Hypothesized).

None of the provided articles mention congenital diaphragmatic hernia or any diaphragm/lung developmental phenotype. The literature on KLK4 centers exclusively on enamel maturation and amelogenesis imperfecta (PMID 25071586, 25153384), evolutionary analyses of enamel genes in mammals and whales (PMID 26596502, 38397217, 26420451), and prostate cancer biology (PMID 11506707). There are no human genetic variant studies, animal models, or pathway data linking KLK4 to diaphragmatic development or herniation. Thus the gene–phenotype pairing appears entirely incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

Human genetic evidence exists: Suzuki et al. (PMID 33131106) reported de novo/mosaic-inherited CELF2 variants in five unrelated individuals, one of whom had intellectual disability with autistic features, and a Chinese ASD WGS cohort identified a likely pathogenic de novo frameshift CELF2 variant (c.1500delT) in a child diagnosed with ASD (PMID 42036727); CELF2 is also listed in SFARI as a syndromic/high-confidence gene (PMID 37891789). However, the dominant clinical phenotype in the larger CELF2 variant cohorts is developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, intellectual disability, and cortical malformation (PMIDs 40666314, 42275152, 34107259), with ASD appearing as a variable associated feature rather than a replicated primary outcome. Supportive but non-human evidence includes Celf2 conditional knockout mice showing autism-like social impairment and synaptic deficits (PMID 38829512) and iPSC organoid work linking CELF2 dysfunction to autism-spectrum neurocognitive phenotypes in DM1 (PMID 35767654). Because the two human reports describe ASD/autistic features as secondary findings within DEE/NDD cohorts rather than independent replicated ASD-causal studies, "Existing" is the most defensible category, with some weight retained for "Established."

No article reports EPS8L1 variants in human patients with congenital heart disease. The 22q11 CNV study (PMID 36777701) concerns chromosome 22q11.2 microdeletions and unrelated genes, not EPS8L1 (19q13), and multigene CNVs would not implicate this gene anyway. The only direct mention of Eps8l1 is as one entry in a differential-expression table from mouse heart tissue/HL-1 cardiomyocytes in an ASXL3-mutation study (PMID 37435360) — murine expression data incidental to the paper's conclusions, providing at most a very weak hypothesis-level link. The EPS8 family characterization paper (PMID 14565974) establishes a role in Rac/actin remodeling, biology that is generically relevant to development but with no cardiac phenotype reported (eps8-null mice are healthy). Overall the evidence is essentially incidental co-mention, favoring Novel with some weight to Hypothesized based on the mouse cardiomyocyte expression change.

Nearly all DSCAML1 literature here concerns neurodevelopmental biology—dendritic self-avoidance, retinal and oculomotor circuit assembly, GABAergic neuron placement, epilepsy, and NDD-associated missense variants—with no cardiac phenotype reported (PMIDs 11453658, 24084194, 25451118, 31685652, 33256836, 33501714, 42003794). The "pathway-based GWAS of coronary heart disease" (PMID 22510845) uses CHD as a homonym for coronary heart disease and does not implicate DSCAML1 in congenital heart disease. The only congenital-heart-disease paper (PMID 31216004) reports abnormal sulcal patterns in single-ventricle CHD with damaging de novo exome variants, but does not name DSCAML1 as a causal gene in its abstract; at most DSCAML1 could be one of many incidental de novo candidates, which is not credible evidence of causation. Related DSCAM (chromosome 21) has been loosely tied to Down syndrome cardiac phenotypes, offering only a tenuous biological rationale that does not extend to DSCAML1. No human proband or family evidence links DSCAML1 variants to congenital heart disease, so Established is excluded.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo, single-gene BRSK2 variants in probands with autism/neurodevelopmental disorder: PMID 30879638 identified nine unrelated probands with rare heterozygous (mostly de novo, loss-of-function) BRSK2 variants with autism and DD/ID; PMID 31452935 (SPARK exome study) found BRSK2 reaching genome-wide significance as an ASD risk gene; PMID 42509346 assembled 52 heterozygous BRSK2 cases with NDD and functional validation; PMIDs 38519481/37961520 reported two de novo damaging SNVs in BRSK2 in ASD families; and case reports (PMIDs 37671287, 41423339) describe de novo frameshift variants in ASD patients with functional support. These constitute replicated, gene-specific (non-CNV) human genetic evidence from independent cohorts. Zebrafish (PMIDs 35754711, 38003696) and biochemical kinase studies add mechanistic support but are not needed for the human causal claim. A small residue of probability is kept for "Existing" given that some articles are case reports or cohorts primarily phenotypic in focus.

None of the provided articles mention congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) or any diaphragmatic structural defect. The NALCN literature consistently describes neurodevelopmental phenotypes: IHPRF1 (biallelic loss-of-function) and CLIFAHDD (gain-of-function), with features such as hypotonia, intellectual disability, distal arthrogryposis, epilepsy, and respiratory rhythm abnormalities (central apnea, periodic breathing) (PMIDs 24075186, 23749988, 29168298, 40048676, 29610177, 29968795, 27844033). Respiratory distress and apnea in these patients are of central/neurogenic origin rather than due to diaphragmatic herniation, so they do not constitute a recognized precursor or mechanism for CDH. A small amount of probability is retained for "Hypothesized" because contracture/arthrogryposis phenotypes and impaired diaphragmatic/respiratory muscle drive could conceivably be argued as biologically relevant, but no such link is made in these abstracts. No human genetic evidence supports a NALCN–CDH association, so Novel is the best fit.

Guo et al. (PMID 33157009) assembled 21 affected individuals from 20 unrelated families with truncating, structural, or disruptive missense NCKAP1 variants (including 8 de novo), showing ASD/autistic features, language and motor delay, plus supporting expression and mouse electroporation data — this is primary human genetic evidence in multiple independent probands. Independent replication comes from additional single-patient and familial reports: a de novo frameshift (p.Ser986Hisfs*34) with autistic traits and CHD (PMID 41462819), an adult with a pathogenic NCKAP1 variant and ASD (PMID 40551827), a father–daughter splice-site variant (c.2021+1G>A) with autistic features (PMID 41531171), and diagnostic confirmation in routine testing (PMID 36553572). Earlier work also reported a mosaic disruptive NCKAP1 mutation in an ASD proband (PMID 27632392) and a segregating truncating variant in an ID family (PMID 28940097). NCKAP1 is a SFARI score-1 high-confidence ASD gene, and mechanistic WAVE-complex studies (PMID 39660913) support biological plausibility. A small residual probability remains for "Existing" since several reports are single cases and the original study itself noted the need for further replication.

None of the provided articles report congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) in association with SEC23A. The SEC23A literature consistently concerns cranio-lenticulo-sutural dysplasia (craniofacial, skeletal, lens, and growth phenotypes) and COPII-mediated ER-to-Golgi trafficking, plus functional overlap with SEC23B in congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II (CDAII — an acronym distinct from CDH). Reported patient phenotypes include fontanel, cataract, skeletal, cardiac, and neurological features, but no diaphragmatic defects. A weak biological rationale could be argued since COPII-dependent collagen/ECM secretion affects connective tissue and mesenchymal development, which is relevant to diaphragm formation, giving a small share to Hypothesized. Otherwise the co-mentions are incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

None of the provided articles address congenital diaphragmatic hernia in any way. The FGF12 literature here is dominated by developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (recurrent p.Arg52His/p.Arg114His variants, duplications) and, secondarily, orofacial clefting associations in Scandinavian cleft cohorts. There is no report of diaphragmatic defects, diaphragm development, or lung/diaphragm morphogenesis linked to FGF12 in these abstracts, and no animal model or pathway evidence connecting FGF12 to diaphragm formation. A small residual probability is left for "Hypothesized" because FGF signaling broadly participates in mesenchymal development, but nothing in this evidence base supports even a biological hypothesis specific to CDH.

Multiple independent human studies report sequence-level (not merely CNV) SHANK2 variants in ASD probands: Berkel et al. (PMID 20473310) found a de novo nonsense mutation plus rare inherited missense changes specific to ASD/ID cases after sequencing 396 patients; Leblond et al. (PMID 22346768) independently sequenced 455 patients and found significant enrichment of rare damaging variants in ASD cases versus controls with functional synaptic validation. A dedicated phenotypic-spectrum report (PMID 32987185) delineates 11 patients with SHANK2 de novo variants whose core features include ASD, and further independent probands are described in PMIDs 41219921, 40057302, and 38704506 (patient-derived Y29X mutation with isogenic iPSC correction). Case-control association data in a Chinese cohort (PMID 29934968) and cross-disorder ADHD/ASD SNP analysis (PMID 33986640) add supporting population-level evidence. This replicated, multi-proband human evidence with de novo point mutations supports an Established causal relationship, with residual probability on Existing given heterogeneity and incomplete penetrance/multiple-hit considerations.

No article reports KLF2 variants in human congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) patients or families, so Established and Existing are not supported. The strongest evidence is animal/functional: LKLF (KLF2) is significantly down-regulated in the nitrofen-induced rat CDH model of pulmonary hypoplasia (PMID 21053160), and Klf2-null mice/chimeras show defective lung development (PMID 10409672), with Klf2 required for type I pneumocyte differentiation (PMID 22001906). These data give a biologically plausible, directly relevant mechanistic link to the pulmonary hypoplasia central to CDH pathophysiology, fitting "Hypothesized." Other listed papers concern pulmonary arterial hypertension gene panels, cerebral cavernous malformations, or mechanotransduction and are incidental co-mentions of KLF2 unrelated to CDH.

The only provided article (PMID 14565974) characterizes the eps8 family, including EPS8L1, as regulators of Rac-mediated actin cytoskeletal remodeling in fibroblasts and mice; it makes no mention of congenital diaphragmatic hernia or any diaphragm/lung developmental phenotype. There are no human genetic studies, no patient variants, and no probands or families linking EPS8L1 to CDH, so Established and Existing are not supportable. A small amount of weight is given to Hypothesized because actin cytoskeletal/Rac signaling is broadly relevant to mesenchymal cell migration during diaphragm development, but this is a generic pathway link rather than a specific, phenotype-relevant biological argument. Overall the evidence base is essentially an incidental co-mention, consistent with a Novel gene–disease relationship.

All retrieved articles concern RHOBTB2 variants in developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, alternating hemiplegia of childhood, paroxysmal movement disorders, dystonia, and Rett-like phenotypes. None of the abstracts mention congenital diaphragmatic hernia, diaphragm development, lung hypoplasia, or any related structural birth defect of the diaphragm. There is no human genetic evidence, no animal model, and no biological pathway link connecting RHOBTB2 to diaphragmatic hernia in this literature set; the Drosophila work addresses dendritic/neurological function only. Therefore the gene–phenotype pair appears entirely unsupported, warranting a "Novel" classification with only residual probability given to weaker categories.

Human evidence exists but is limited: the large CHD cohort study of 11,555 probands (PMID 40127276) reports damaging de novo mutations in LHX2 in two probands with aortic and mitral atresia, citing mouse knockout CHD as supporting rationale, and a Chinese Han LVOTO whole-exome study (PMID 38164514) lists LHX2 among 32 burden-enriched candidate genes with a recurrent missense variant (though its presence in 22 individuals raises concern it is a common variant rather than a causal allele). An ENU mouse screen combined with human probands also lists LHX2 among neuronal/transcription-factor candidates (PMID 39135118), and mouse knockout data (pharyngeal mesoderm, outflow tract/DiGeorge-like phenotypes) provide a strong biological mechanism. Human LHX2 variant studies otherwise focus on neurodevelopmental disorder, micro/anophthalmia and schizencephaly (PMIDs 37057675, 21203406, 20949537), with no cardiac phenotype, so no replicated clinical causal demonstration of CHD exists. Therefore Existing is most appropriate, with substantial residual weight on Hypothesized given the reliance on candidate-gene/burden signals and animal models.

None of the provided articles mention congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) at all; they cover PCBP2 biology in iron homeostasis, RNA splicing/stability, cancer, viral translation, trophoblast differentiation, and adipogenesis. The only human variant-level evidence (PMID 38965372) implicates de novo PCBP2 variants in neurodevelopmental disorders with motor and language delay, which is not a recognized precursor, subtype, or mechanism of CDH. The trophoblast/placental and developmental splicing work (PMID 34095140) establishes a general developmental regulatory role, which offers only a weak, indirect biological rationale rather than a CDH-specific hypothesis. No clinical studies in CDH probands or families exist here, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded; a small weight goes to Hypothesized given PCBP2's broad roles in cell proliferation, migration, and differentiation relevant to tissue morphogenesis.

Human genetic data link MOV10 to ASD but fall short of replicated causal proof: the BARAKA-Qatar WGS study (PMID 37805537) reports a de novo predicted loss-of-function variant in MOV10 (pLI > 0.99) in an ASD proband as a novel candidate gene, the NMD-pathway study (PMID 35327467) identified three damaging SNVs in MOV10 helicase/CH domains in ASD patients, and the cross-disorder gene-prioritization work (PMID 26817790) ranks MOV10 in tier 2 with two de novo pLOF variants across developmental brain disorders including ASD. However, these are candidate-level or aggregate analyses rather than independent clinical confirmations of causation, and the CNV-based overlap study (PMID 24954825) involves a multigene duplication that cannot implicate MOV10 specifically. Strong supporting biology comes from mouse/cell work showing Mov10 regulates neurite outgrowth, dendritic arborization, retroelement suppression, and interacts with FMRP/AGO2 (PMIDs 28662698, 31740951, 27338369), which would alone support only "Hypothesized." Taken together, the limited but credible human variant evidence places this at "Existing," with residual probability on "Hypothesized."

No article reports SEPTIN2 variants in patients with congenital heart disease; the only human SEPTIN2 variant study (PMID 41408595) links mutations to cognitive impairment via axon initial segment dysfunction, not cardiac malformation. The strongest cardiac-relevant data come from mouse endocardial conditional knockouts, where Septin2 (and Septin9) deletion produced no detectable abnormality, while only Septin7 caused valve disease (PMID 42657464) — effectively negative evidence for SEPTIN2. Human SEPTIN2 associations are with acquired adult disease: reduced septin-2 in myxomatous mitral degeneration (PMID 25232280) and S-nitrosylated Septin2 in aortic aneurysm/dissection (PMID 38357802), neither of which is congenital heart disease. Generic biological plausibility exists through septin roles at the ciliary base and cilia's central role in CHD (PMIDs 24317785, 28159874), supporting a Hypothesized rather than Existing classification, though the negative knockout result tempers this and keeps meaningful weight on Novel.

No article in this set reports PCBP2 variants in CHD probands or families, so an Established call is impossible (no candidate PMIDs exist for causal variant evidence). The strongest link is PMID 35984151, a human bioinformatic study of CHD patient tissue and CHD-iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes in which PCBP2 is predicted as an RNA-binding protein regulating CHD-associated alternative splicing events (e.g., IRF7), which is functional/transcriptomic rather than genetic evidence. PMID 38556427 is a review that merely cites PCBP2 as part of a reported "CHD gene network," a background citation rather than primary variant evidence, which supports at most a modest Existing weight. The remaining papers concern PCBP2 biology in iron homeostasis, miRNA processing, IRES translation, cancer, Alzheimer's, and adipogenesis, providing general mechanistic plausibility (RBP/splicing regulation relevant to cardiogenesis) but no CHD-specific genetic data. Therefore the evidence best fits Hypothesized, with residual probability for Existing and Novel.

H1-4 (HIST1H1E) frameshift variants cause Rahman syndrome, and the largest phenotypic series of 30 individuals lists cardiac anomalies among associated clinical features (PMID 31400068), providing human evidence that variants in this gene can contribute to congenital heart defects as part of a syndrome. Additional supportive but weak human data include a de novo HIST1H1E missense variant of uncertain significance identified in a CHD patient in the Sidra Cardiac Registry (PMID 36011280) and an array-CGH study nominating HIST1H1E as a candidate for conotruncal anomalies (PMID 35045913) — the latter is a multigene CNV and cannot single out this gene. The remaining literature concerns neurodevelopmental phenotypes, overgrowth/intellectual disability, senescence, lymphoma, and in vitro chromatin biophysics, which supports biological plausibility (chromatin/epigenetic regulation is a known CHD mechanism) rather than direct causation of CHD. Because no two independent studies report CHD-causing point variants in distinct probands as their own primary finding, Established is not warranted; the evidence best fits "Existing" with substantial residual weight on "Hypothesized."

Human DNM1L variants are reported only for EMPF1-type encephalopathy with neurological phenotypes (PMIDs 30801875, 33387674, 36763487, 38481935), with no congenital heart malformations attributed to these variants, so Established and Existing cannot be supported by patient genetic data. However, there is strong, directly relevant biology: DRP1/DNM1L-mediated mitochondrial fission was shown to be required for oxygen sensing and ductus arteriosus constriction/closure using human DA tissue from infants undergoing CHD repair (PMID 23334860), which mechanistically links DNM1L to patent ductus arteriosus. Additional supportive but indirect data include altered DRP1 in pressure-overload right ventricular failure modeling tetralogy of Fallot (PMID 33522250), zebrafish cardiac developmental toxicity involving Drp1/Fis1 imbalance (PMID 41687852), and mitophagy/fission interplay in TAMM41-related heart valve development (PMID 30824836). These constitute pathway, expression, and animal/ex vivo functional evidence without causal variant data, placing the relationship firmly in the Hypothesized category, with a small residual possibility that the co-mentions are incidental (Novel).

Multiple human studies report their own patient-level variant data: PMID 37195288 describes 12 individuals with heterozygous de novo loss-of-function ANK2 variants presenting with a neurodevelopmental syndrome including autism spectrum disorder and epilepsy; PMID 40035441 identifies a novel de novo nonsense variant (p.R1003*) in a proband with ASD/epilepsy and summarizes 16 reported patients; PMID 37088467 reports a new ANK2 mutation in a patient with autism; and PMID 39978592 describes a familial missense variant segregating with ASD and subthreshold autistic traits. These are single-gene sequence variants (not multigene CNVs) in independent probands/families, consistent with replication, and ANK2 is repeatedly cited as a high-confidence ASD risk gene from large exome studies (PMID 39631164, 35990955). Some supporting evidence is in vitro (hiPSC neurons) or review-based, and expressivity is variable with missense variants of uncertain significance, so a residual probability remains for "Existing".

No article reports a single-gene (sequence-level) FGF12 variant causing congenital heart disease; all FGF12 point mutations in this set (p.Arg52His, p.Gly112Ser, p.Glu153Gly) cause epileptic encephalopathy, not CHD. Human CHD evidence is limited to multigenic copy-number variants: an FGF12-containing CNV in classic heterotaxy (PMID 27637763), a CNV near FGF12 in Ebstein anomaly (PMID 29216221), and FGF12 within a large 3q26-29 gain in VSD cases (PMID 26742958), plus an epigenetic DMR association in Down-syndrome CHD (PMID 37803336). Because these CNVs span many genes and cannot isolate FGF12, they support "Existing" (credible but non-definitive human association) rather than "Established." Additional support is largely biological/pathway-based (atrial Fgf12 expression, Xenopus modeling of candidate CHD genes), which justifies substantial weight on "Hypothesized."

None of the provided articles mention congenital diaphragmatic hernia or any diaphragm/lung developmental phenotype. The DSCAML1 literature here is exclusively neurodevelopmental: axon/dendrite guidance, retinal patterning, oculomotor function, synapse formation, epilepsy/GABAergic neuron placement, and reproductive traits in goats. The only human variant studies (PMIDs 33501714, 33256836) link DSCAML1 to neurodevelopmental disorders and epilepsy, not to CDH, and provide no mechanistic or pathway basis for diaphragm morphogenesis. There is therefore no evidence—genetic, expression, or model-organism—connecting DSCAML1 to congenital diaphragmatic hernia, making the relationship Novel.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo or segregating single-nucleotide KCNB1 variants in probands with autism spectrum disorder: PMID 29264390 characterizes a KCNB1 p.Ile199Phe variant in a proband with autism, ID and epilepsy with supporting electrophysiology; PMID 39135902 reports a sibling pair (and carrier father with autistic features) with a novel KCNB1 p.S114R variant causing ASD plus functional channel defects; PMID 31696658 identified a pathogenic de novo KCNB1 missense variant in an ASD proband from a Brazilian trio cohort; ASD-focused sequencing studies (PMID 38256266, 40169255) independently report de novo KCNB1 variants as primary diagnostic findings in ASD probands. Large phenotyping series (PMID 32954514, 34915430) further show autistic features in ~56% and ASD risk in 13/18 KCNB1 patients, supporting ASD as a core part of the KCNB1 encephalopathy spectrum. The main caveat is that ASD usually occurs within a broader developmental/epileptic encephalopathy phenotype rather than as isolated autism, which leaves some weight on "Existing." Animal/in vitro data alone would not suffice, but here the electrophysiological work supplements human proband-level genetic evidence.

The literature provides multiple human genetic studies linking GABRB3 to ASD: linkage disequilibrium and TDT association with the 155CA-2 microsatellite (PMID 9545402, 11920158), transmission distortion in Korean trios (PMID 19430570), a maternally transmitted rare signal-peptide variant P11S with functional characterization (PMID 19935738), excess of rare 5'-regulatory and coding variants in patients versus controls (PMID 24999380), and association with Asperger syndrome and autism-related endophenotypes (PMID 24321478). However, these are association/transmission findings rather than demonstrations of causation, several are in small samples, and a meta-analysis (PMID 29725984) found no significant association for common GABA receptor SNPs, with other reports negative (PMID 37019319).
