The remaining supporting evidence comes from multigenic 15q11-q13 duplications/deletions and epigenetic dysregulation, which cannot isolate GABRB3 from its neighbours, and SFARI category listings are background citations rather than primary causal evidence. Therefore the weight falls on "Existing," with some residual probability for "Established" given the breadth of independent human cohorts reporting rare and common variant associations.

None of the provided articles mention congenital diaphragmatic hernia or any diaphragmatic/lung developmental phenotype. The DNM1L literature here is entirely about mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission biology (PMIDs 11553726, 15208300, 11703942, 15452144) and the human disease EMPF1 — encephalopathy due to defective mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission — with neurological phenotypes such as epileptic encephalopathy, dystonia, sensory neuropathy and ataxia (PMIDs 17460227, 30801875, 33387674, 38481935, 36763487). No patient variants, animal models, or mechanistic pathways linking DNM1L to diaphragm development or CDH are described. There is at most a very weak indirect rationale (mitochondrial dysfunction in multisystem congenital syndromes), so a small amount of probability is left for "Hypothesized," but the overwhelming likelihood is that the relationship is Novel.

None of the LHX2 articles address diaphragm development or congenital diaphragmatic hernia; they concern forebrain patterning, axon guidance, eye/olfactory development, schizencephaly, pituitary anomalies, and a neurodevelopmental disorder from LHX2 haploinsufficiency (PMID 37057675), which lists no diaphragmatic defects. The only CDH article (PMID 36816370) is a clinical study of inotropic scores and makes no mention of LHX2 or any genetics. Thus the gene and phenotype are merely co-listed with no shared biology, pathway, or animal-model evidence provided. A small probability is retained for "hypothesized" because LHX2 is a developmental LIM-homeobox transcription factor expressed in limb/fin buds and mesenchyme, which could conceivably be relevant, but nothing in this literature set supports it.

The only provided article concerns C. elegans Q neuroblast polarization and migration involving UNC-40/DCC, MIG-21, DPY-19 and Fat-like cadherins. The "CDH" mentions (CDH-3, CDH-4) are cadherin gene names, a homonym for the congenital diaphragmatic hernia acronym, and should be dismissed. There is no mention of the histone gene H2BC8 (HIST1H2BG) nor any human genetic, expression, or functional evidence linking it to congenital diaphragmatic hernia. With no relevant evidence at all, the relationship is best classified as Novel.

The strongest human evidence is the large sequencing study of 11,555 CHD probands (PMID 40127276), where NR6A1 appears among genes with a significant burden of damaging heterozygous variants and is discussed as a novel CHD candidate—this is a single, credible human genetic study supporting "Existing" but not replicated independently. Other human NR6A1 variant studies establish an oculo-vertebral-renal syndrome and CAKUT (PMIDs 40610405, 39606449, 40774958, 41733738), phenotypes that are extracardiac, although these confirm NR6A1 as a developmental disease gene and note co-occurring developmental/cardiac phenotypes in the cohort. The de novo 9q33.3 duplication in pulmonary atresia (PMID 24826987) spans NR5A1 and NR6A1 and cannot implicate NR6A1 specifically. Supporting but non-human/mechanistic evidence includes miR-377-3p/NR6A1 regulation of placental macrophages in MC-LR-induced CHD in mice (PMID 39053546), upregulation in embryos of diabetic mice (PMID 29286097), and cardiac fibrosis modifier mapping in BXD mice (PMID 33529666). Since no two independent human studies report NR6A1 point variants causing CHD, "Established" is not warranted.

None of the provided articles report congenital diaphragmatic hernia in association with NR6A1. The human genetic evidence links NR6A1 variants to oculo-vertebral-renal syndrome (coloboma/microphthalmia, vertebral and kidney anomalies) and to CAKUT (PMIDs 40610405, 39606449, 40774958), and other human work ties it to vertebral number variation (PMID 41261143); a 9q33-q34 deletion case involves multiple genes and is non-specific (PMID 17431898). Mouse and Xenopus knockout/knockdown studies show NR6A1 is required for somitogenesis, posterior axis formation, neural tube closure and gut closure (PMIDs 11134352, 12729562), which provides only an indirect, speculative mechanistic bridge to diaphragm (pleuroperitoneal fold/somite-derived muscle) development. Because this plausible developmental link is tenuous and there is no reported diaphragmatic phenotype in any species or patient here, the relationship is best described as Novel, with modest weight for Hypothesized.

The only article linking NEDD9 to a seizure phenotype is a retrospective aCGH study in 80 epilepsy patients (PMID 33484953), which nominates NEDD9 (along with RASAL2 and TNR) as a candidate epilepsy gene based on copy number variants, several of which were classified as variants of unknown significance. This is human data but represents a hypothesis-generating CNV finding spanning genomic regions that cannot isolate NEDD9 from neighbouring genes, and the phenotype is epilepsy broadly rather than epileptic encephalopathy specifically; no replication in independent probands or families exists. All other listed articles concern NEDD9/HEF1/Cas-L biology in integrin, TCR, BCR-ABL, retinoic acid, ciliary, cancer and pulmonary hypertension contexts, providing no epilepsy-relevant mechanism, although the retinoic-acid–regulated neurodevelopmental and neurite outgrowth roles (PMIDs 18585997, 25120220) give weak biological plausibility. Established is effectively excluded since no paper reports causal single-gene variants in patients with epileptic encephalopathy.

No article in the list reports variants in H2BC8 (HIST1H2BG) in patients with congenital heart disease, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. The "CHD remodelers" paper (PMID 42439481) uses CHD as the acronym for chromodomain-helicase-DNA-binding proteins and neurodevelopmental syndromes, a homonym that must be dismissed. The epigenetics/genetics reviews (PMIDs 35348004, 33803261, 34209044, 33294766) discuss chromatin modification generally but do not implicate this specific histone cluster gene. The only tangential biological link is PMID 41145490, where RNF20-mediated histone H2B monoubiquitination (H2Bub1) in cardiac endothelium is required for normal heart development—this makes H2B biology plausibly relevant to cardiogenesis, supporting a modest Hypothesized weight, but the evidence concerns RNF20 in mouse models, not H2BC8 variants in humans.

The great majority of CHAMP1 papers describe a neurodevelopmental syndrome (intellectual disability, autism, microcephaly, hypotonia, seizures, GI issues) with no consistent report of congenital heart defects (PMIDs 26751395, 34021018, 36797464, 37454340, 41111978). Several of the "congenital heart disease" articles retrieved are homonym hits, where "CHAMP" denotes the Cardiac High Acuity Monitoring Program or a trekking/camp context (PMIDs 40470120, 41602892, 42212184, 41027595), and should be dismissed. The only human genetic datapoint is a NICU cohort in which CHAMP1 appears in a list of single-nucleotide-variant molecular diagnoses among infants with CHD (PMID 38499751), a single incidental case without phenotypic detail; the 13q33-q34 microdeletion series notes heart anomalies in 10–30% of patients, but these are multigene CNVs that cannot implicate CHAMP1 specifically (PMID 31321490). Functional work shows CHAMP1 acts in mitotic chromosome alignment and as a MyoD cofactor in skeletal myoblast fusion (PMID 41540007), offering only indirect, non-cardiac biological plausibility. Evidence therefore falls between weak "Existing" (one borderline human report) and "Novel," with no basis for "Established."

The H1-4 (HIST1H1E) literature is dominated by Rahman syndrome — frameshift variants in the C-terminal tail causing intellectual disability, distinctive facies, overgrowth, premature aging, and occasional skeletal/cardiac anomalies (PMIDs 28475857, 31400068, 31447100, 33270410) — with no report of congenital diaphragmatic hernia in any proband. The only article co-mentioning diaphragmatic hernia is a UK Biobank adult height Mendelian randomisation study (PMID 30355295), where HIST1H1E merely appears within a large "protein kinase A signalling" pathway gene list for adult (acquired/hiatal-type) diaphragmatic hernia, not a congenital malformation, and no variant-level association to CDH is reported. Other papers are purely mechanistic/in vitro (chromatin compaction, phase separation; PMIDs 34788807, 42173878) or involve unrelated phenotypes (ovarian cancer, craniosynostosis, spontaneous abortion CNVs spanning the histone cluster), the latter being multigene CNVs that cannot implicate H1-4 specifically. There is therefore no human genetic evidence linking H1-4 variants to CDH, and only a very weak, pathway-level biological rationale, so Novel is most likely with a modest allowance for Hypothesized.

No article in this set reports ALYREF variants in patients with congenital heart disease. The strongest human genetic evidence (PMID 34547244) identifies ALYREF as a de novo candidate risk gene for congenital diaphragmatic hernia — a different congenital anomaly, although one that frequently co-occurs with and shares developmental pathways with cardiac malformations, which gives a weak, indirect basis for a hypothesized link. PMID 42781784 places ALYREF within a TREX-subunit neurodevelopmental disability spectrum, with cognitive, speech, respiratory and dysmorphic features, and arthrogryposis attributable to THOC2 rather than ALYREF; no cardiac phenotype is attributed to ALYREF. The remaining ALYREF papers concern mRNA export, EJC assembly, TREX assembly, PI3K/Akt signaling and ALS/FTD, with no cardiac relevance, and the congenital heart disease papers (screening, prevalence, endocarditis, maternal age/Nkx2-5) do not mention ALYREF. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel, with meaningful probability mass given to Hypothesized because of the shared "constrained developmental gene" and congenital-anomaly context.

All SOX10-specific articles concern Waardenburg syndrome types 2/4, Hirschsprung disease, PCWH, hypomyelinating leukodystrophy and melanoma—none report SOX10 variants in congenital diaphragmatic hernia patients (PMIDs 34667088, 20127975, 33251892, 40702859). The CDH-related papers mention SOX10 only incidentally as a neural crest marker: in the rat scRNA-seq CDH study it is merely a cell-type annotation marker, and in the mouse diaphragm morphogenesis paper SOX10 is used as a negative control showing no overlap with migrating muscle progenitors (PMIDs 41246903, 29679560). Other CDH papers (FREM1, MYRF) cite SOX10 only as a transcriptional regulator of MYRF in oligodendrocytes, which is background rather than evidence for CDH (PMIDs 23221805, 29446546). Thus there are no human genetic data and essentially no mechanistic argument tying SOX10 to diaphragm defects, so the relationship is best described as Novel, with a modest allowance for Hypothesized given SOX10's role in neural crest derivatives that contribute to structures near the developing diaphragm.

The strongest primary human evidence is the Meacham syndrome series (PMID 17853480), where two patients with complex congenital heart defects and diaphragmatic malformations carried heterozygous C-terminal zinc-finger WT1 missense mutations (Arg366Cys, Arg394Trp), with a proposed coelomic mesothelial/proepicardial mechanism. A second report (PMID 15191353) describes a WT1 P181S carrier with coarctation of the aorta and PDA, but the authors themselves argue the cardiac defect was likely coincidental, weakening it as replication. Other WT1 papers (Denys-Drash, Frasier, WT1-related disorders, nephrotic syndrome/CDH cases) focus on renal, gonadal, and diaphragmatic phenotypes and mention cardiac involvement only incidentally or as background, and the epicardial/EpiMT and wt1−/− mouse data (PMIDs 42677159, 21985433) support biological plausibility rather than variant-level human causation. Therefore the balance favors "Existing" — credible but limited human genetic evidence, essentially resting on a single multi-proband series — with meaningful residual probability for "Established" and for purely mechanistic/"Hypothesized" interpretation.

Human genetic evidence exists: the large genomic analysis of 11,555 CHD probands (PMID 40127276) reported a significant burden of damaging heterozygous variants in KLF2 associated with a specific CHD phenotype, and the trio-based transcription-factor burden meta-analysis (PMID 41022857) identified KLF2 as a novel candidate CHD gene, while explicitly noting it "has not been directly associated with CHD" previously. Additionally, PMID 40858839 states that dominant loss-of-function and damaging missense KLF2 variants were previously identified in patients with aortic/mitral valve defects and hypoplastic left heart syndrome, and a 2023–2025 scoping review (PMID 42724214) lists KLF2 among reported candidate CHD genes. However, these cohorts may overlap (PCGC-type datasets), the gene is still described as candidate-level rather than definitively causal, and much supporting mechanism comes from zebrafish klf2a/mouse mechanosensitive valve biology (PMIDs 29364115, 38748804, 41049289). This supports "Existing" most strongly, with meaningful but not decisive probability for "Established."

The only article linking CHAMP1 to congenital diaphragmatic hernia is the DECIPHER-based CDH+ study (PMID 35904974), where a single subject with CDH plus other anomalies carried a pathogenic CHAMP1 frameshift variant (c.1741delG, p.Glu581Asnfs*4); notably, CHAMP1 was not among the genes the authors nominated as supported diaphragm-development candidates (CREBBP, SMARCA4, UBA2, USP9X). All other CHAMP1 papers (PMIDs 26340335, 26751395, 34021018, 36797464, 37454340, etc.) describe a neurodevelopmental disorder phenotype with no mention of diaphragmatic hernia, and the remaining CDH papers mention only cAMP/cGMP homonyms rather than the gene. Thus there is a single human proband and no replication, which precludes "Established," and the human genetic observation makes "Hypothesized" less apt than "Existing," though the incidental, unemphasized nature of that single case leaves meaningful probability for "Novel."

The only primary human genetic evidence comes from Qiao et al. (PMID 34547244), which identified ALYREF as a candidate CDH-associated gene based on de novo coding variant enrichment reaching FDR < 0.05 in 827 CDH trios; notably, that study's functional follow-up focused on LONP1, not ALYREF. Subsequent mentions in reviews (PMIDs 35186825, 34573387, 42125881) restate this single finding as background rather than providing independent replication in new probands or families. The remaining ALYREF literature concerns mRNA export/TREX biology, ALS/FTD, or THOC6 intellectual disability syndrome, and a TREX-spectrum neurodevelopmental cohort (PMID 42781784) that does not report CDH. With only one primary human study and no replication or functional CDH model, the evidence supports "Existing" rather than "Established."

The only provided article concerns CTRP6 (C1QTNF6) mRNA stability under mitochondrial DNA depletion in murine C2C12 muscle cells, relating to fatty acid metabolism — with no mention of epilepsy, seizures, or epileptic encephalopathy. No human genetic variant studies, patient cohorts, or neurological phenotypes link C1QTNF6 to epileptic encephalopathy. There is not even a plausible biological pathway argument presented connecting this gene to epileptogenesis, so "Hypothesized" is barely supported (only via a tenuous mitochondrial-dysfunction angle). Therefore the evidence overwhelmingly supports a "Novel" classification.

No article in this set reports point mutations in SOX10 found in patients whose primary phenotype is congenital heart disease; the human SOX10 literature here concerns Waardenburg syndrome, Hirschsprung disease, and Kallmann syndrome (PMIDs 20127975, 34667088, 30914325, 33251892), which are neurocristopathies but not CHD. The only human CHD-linked report (PMID 32703023) is a 1.99 Mb 22q12.3-q13.1 deletion spanning SOX10 plus 13 other RefSeq genes, which cannot attribute the heart defect to SOX10 specifically, so it cannot support "Established" and only weakly supports "Existing". The remaining support is biological: SOX10 is a canonical cardiac neural crest marker implicated in outflow tract septation and conotruncal defects in reviews and animal/zebrafish models (PMIDs 41049289, 41571667, 38892128), and SoxE genes are expressed in developing valves and cardiac autonomic nerves (noted in PMID 35218327). Because that evidence is model-organism/expression-based rather than human variant-based, most weight falls on Hypothesized, with a substantial minority for Existing given the contiguous-gene-deletion case.

No article in this set reports ANK1 variants in patients with epileptic encephalopathy; the epilepsy-specific papers concern KCNQ2 (PMIDs 27905566, 28100740) and SHANK1 (PMID 34912368), and the rare-variant burden study (PMID 37369202) highlights other genes (HSPG2, FLNA, TNC), so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. Human ANK1 evidence relates to hereditary spherocytosis and erythrocyte cytoskeleton biology (PMIDs 33410423, 23934996, 27848995, 30279439), not seizures. The only neurologically relevant data are from mice: nb/nb erythroid ankyrin deficiency causes Purkinje cell loss and a psychomotor syndrome (PMID 1716634), and Ank1 transcripts are expressed in cerebellum — a plausible but indirect, non-epileptic CNS link that provides only weak support for a "Hypothesized" relationship. Overall the gene–phenotype co-mention appears largely incidental, favoring Novel with secondary weight on Hypothesized.

The strongest human evidence is PMID 37552066, which reports 12 individuals with de novo RAB5C variants; notably, the two patients with loss-of-function variants had refractory epilepsy with intellectual disability, while missense carriers showed macrocephaly/developmental delay, with supporting in vitro, C. elegans and zebrafish functional work. Additional human support comes from targeted sequencing of candidate genes in an epileptic encephalopathy cohort reporting a dominant RAB5C p.W130X variant (PMID 27652284) and from the NPdenovo de novo mutation compilation listing RAB5C as an EE candidate gene (PMID 25849321). However, the epilepsy phenotype is driven by only two LoF probands in a single study, and the other reports are candidate-level or database-derived rather than definitive causal demonstrations, so replication specific to epileptic encephalopathy is limited. Remaining papers (RAB5 biology, VWF trafficking, nephrotic syndrome, Wnt11/gastrulation) are mechanistic or unrelated and support at most a biological plausibility layer. This places the evidence solidly in "Existing," with some probability of "Established."

None of the provided articles mention congenital diaphragmatic hernia at all; the literature concerns septin cytoskeletal biology (filament assembly, SUMOylation, ciliary localization, bacterial invasion, sperm head–tail junction, erythrocyte membrane properties). The only human variant study implicating SEPTIN2 (PMID 41408595) links mutations to axon initial segment dysfunction and cognitive impairment, not to diaphragm development or herniation. Mouse conditional knockouts of Septin2 showed no detectable abnormalities (PMID 42657464), arguing against a developmental structural phenotype. There is therefore no direct, indirect, or model-organism evidence connecting SEPTIN2 variation to CDH; a small weight is retained for "hypothesized" only because septins participate in cytoskeletal/planar-cell-polarity processes relevant to morphogenesis (PMID 20671153).

Multiple independent human probands carry point (non-CNV) WT1 variants together with diaphragmatic defects: PMID 7645607 (Denys-Drash newborn with large diaphragmatic hernia and WT1 p.Arg366His), PMID 18203154 (a third independent DDS case with CDH and the same Arg366His mutation), PMID 16932893 (DDS infant with Arg366His and a diaphragmatic defect), and PMID 10792605 (intron 9 splice-site mutation in a boy with FSGS plus diaphragmatic hernia). These are complemented by trio exome sequencing of CDH fetuses reporting likely damaging de novo WT1 variants (PMID 34315577) and by WT1 mutations described in Meacham syndrome, which includes CDH. WAGR 11p13 deletion cases (PMIDs 15779010, 17194330) are supportive but multigenic and do not isolate WT1. The main caveat is PMID 8811558, which found no WT1 mutations in isolated CDH, suggesting WT1 mainly causes syndromic CDH; nonetheless, replicated human sequence-variant evidence supports an Established relationship, with residual probability on Existing.

The only provided article is a mouse knockout study of the FAM134 family (FAM134A/RETREG2, FAM134B, FAM134C) examining ER-phagy and axonal ER architecture; notably, combined deletion involving Fam134a produced no additional phenotype and the observed defects were peripheral neuromuscular/somatosensory degeneration, not epilepsy or encephalopathy. There are no human genetic studies, no patient variants, and no epileptic encephalopathy phenotype reported for RETREG2/FAM134A. At most, one could argue weak biological plausibility because the gene is expressed in neurons and participates in ER homeostasis, a pathway implicated broadly in neurological disease, which supports a small allocation to Hypothesized. No evidence supports Established or Existing, as both require human variant data.

ot_trait: cardiac anomalies - developmental delay - facial dysmorphism syndrome
justification: Several human studies report MED13L sequence variants in patients with severe epilepsy phenotypes: a WES study of developmental and epileptic encephalopathies identified a de novo pathogenic frameshift (c.4670dup, p.Ala1558SerfsTer6) in a DEE proband (PMID 38256219); a West syndrome EEG-biomarker cohort lists a patient with a MED13L mutation (PMID 38903771); and a functional/clinical study of five missense variants correlated exon 15 variants with epilepsy and severe motor impairment (PMID 40500968). Additional cohort/phenotype reviews note seizures and abnormal EEG in 20–50% of MED13L syndrome patients and higher epilepsy incidence with missense variants (PMIDs 28645799, 40389839), and a case report describes an MED13L patient with epileptic diathesis/epileptic encephalopathy (PMID 38968441). However, most of these are single probands, table entries, or restatements within broader ID/DD syndromic descriptions rather than dedicated replicated evidence that MED13L causes epileptic encephalopathy per se, so the evidence is credible but not definitive. This supports "Existing" most strongly, with a meaningful but smaller probability of "Established."

ot_trait: complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations 7
justification: None of the provided articles report epilepsy or epileptic encephalopathy in association with EBF2 variants; no patient cohorts with seizures or developmental and epileptic encephalopathy phenotypes are described. The human genetic evidence is limited to a multigene 8p12-p21.2 interstitial deletion with developmental delay and peripheral neuropathy (PMID 16528753), which cannot implicate EBF2 specifically, and a Kawasaki disease association (PMID 29749135), an unrelated phenotype. The remaining literature is predominantly adipose/thermogenesis biology (EBF2 as brown fat determination factor) or murine/Xenopus neurodevelopmental work on Purkinje cell specification, GnRH neuron migration, and motor neuron differentiation (PMIDs 16774995, 18403128, 30658714, 21220016). These neuronal roles give EBF2 some plausible CNS developmental relevance, supporting a modest "Hypothesized" weight, but there is no mechanistic or expression link to cortical hyperexcitability or epileptogenesis, so "Novel" remains most likely.

The great majority of the listed literature concerns MFN2 and Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2A (axonal neuropathy), which is not epileptic encephalopathy. Two human reports do link MFN2 variants to encephalopathy: a homozygous in-frame exon 16 deletion causing severe antenatal encephalopathy with lissencephaly/polymicrogyria and clumped mitochondria (PMID 37804319), and a severe CMT2 case with fatal encephalopathy due to a novel MFN2 splicing mutation (PMID 20530328). However, neither is explicitly characterized as a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with seizures as the defining feature, so the phenotype match is partial and replication for the specific epileptic encephalopathy phenotype is lacking. Other co-mentions are incidental: the DNM1L epileptic encephalopathy paper (PMID 27145208) cites MFN2 only as background on mitochondrial dynamics, and the HNRNPU/DEE54 case (PMID 38846959) reports only an MFN2 VUS. Biological plausibility is strong (mitochondrial fusion defects cause neurodevelopmental/epileptic phenotypes), supporting substantial weight to Hypothesized, but the two human encephalopathy case reports make Existing the most likely category.

No articles were provided linking THEGL (theg spermatid protein-like) to neurodevelopmental disorder. THEGL is a testis-expressed, spermatid-associated gene with no known role in neurodevelopment. In the absence of any literature—human genetic, functional, or expression-based—there is no evidence supporting a causal or associative relationship. The relationship therefore falls into the Novel category.

KMT2B is firmly established as a cause of childhood-onset complex dystonia (DYT-KMT2B) and neurodevelopmental delay, but the provided literature does not contain multiple independent human studies demonstrating KMT2B variants causing epileptic encephalopathy. The strongest direct human evidence is the Aicardi syndrome exome/genome study (PMID 37628618), which identified a unique de novo KMT2B variant in one female with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, and a single case report of a KMT2B splice variant with ataxia, dystonia and seizures (PMID 34477219) — both limited, single-proband findings. Another report (PMID 37489029) implicates KMT2B only within a multigene 19q deletion in an NDD case, which cannot single out the gene. Reviews (PMIDs 29086067, 36054588, 42297634, 42817183) mention KMT2B alongside epileptic encephalopathy genes as background context rather than providing new causal evidence. This supports "Existing" (limited, non-definitive human evidence) rather than "Established," with some residual probability that the co-mentions are incidental (Novel) or purely biological/pathway-based (Hypothesized).

ot_trait: mitochondrial complex V (ATP synthase) deficiency, nuclear type 4A
justification: Human genetic evidence clearly links ATP5F1A variants to severe neurodevelopmental mitochondrial complex V deficiency, and several reports include seizures/encephalopathy: PMID 23599390 describes two siblings with fatal neonatal mitochondrial encephalopathy from an ATP5A1 (ATP5F1A) mutation with functional complementation, and PMID 42520343 reports a multigenerational family with the recurrent p.Arg207His variant whose phenotype (MC5DN4A) includes neonatal-onset epilepsy and developmental delay. PMID 34954817 adds de novo ATP5F1A variants in a cohort whose phenotypic range included epilepsy with early death, though most ATP5F1A probands in that and later series (PMIDs 40859057, 40276935, 41053757, 41743395) present chiefly with developmental delay, movement disorders, or spastic paraplegia rather than an explicit developmental and epileptic encephalopathy diagnosis. Thus the gene–phenotype relationship for "epileptic encephalopathy" specifically is supported but not definitively replicated as a consistent DEE phenotype, favoring Existing with meaningful probability for Established. Other listed papers (33218272, 35220898, 31086314, 36533136, 35185468, 35621276) use ATP5F1A/ATP5A only as a mitochondrial marker or concern other genes and do not contribute evidence.

All articles that actually address developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (PMIDs 41770211, 41153413, 37107610, 38076278, 38612920) attribute the DEE phenotype to the X-linked SMC1A gene; SMC3 appears only as the obligate dimerization partner in the cohesin ring or as background listing of CdLS genes. No paper here reports SMC3 variants in patients with epileptic encephalopathy: the SMC3 loss-of-function cohort (PMID 38297832) describes growth deficiency, developmental delay and dysmorphism without defining an epileptic encephalopathy, and the holoprosencephaly paper (PMID 31334757) reports SMC3 variants for a different malformation phenotype. The functional SMC3 work (PMID 39085358) concerns cardiac development in mice, so it cannot support Established or Existing. The strongest rationale is biological: SMC3 forms the core heterodimer with SMC1A, whose loss-of-function clearly causes DEE85, giving a direct pathway-level plausibility that supports "Hypothesized," with residual probability for "Novel" since the co-mentions are largely incidental.

The only human genetic evidence is a single report of two unrelated individuals sharing the same de novo MIDEAS p.Tyr654Ser variant (PMID: 41290615), but the described phenotype is a multisystem neurodevelopmental syndrome with speech delay, joint contractures, dysmorphism and gut dysmotility — seizures or epileptic encephalopathy are not reported. The remaining papers (PMIDs 35820704, 40966515, 38781120) are purely molecular/structural studies of the MiDAC complex (HDAC1/2, DNTTIP1, MLL3/4, HIV transcription), with mouse data showing MiDAC is essential for embryonic development and neurite outgrowth, which supports only a biologically plausible, indirect link to neurodevelopmental/epileptic phenotypes. No article in this list demonstrates MIDEAS variants in patients with epileptic encephalopathy, so Established is not supportable, and Existing is only weakly supported by the neurodevelopmental overlap. The strongest justified category is Hypothesized, based on chromatin-regulatory biology and neurodevelopmental animal model data, with residual probability for Existing (neurodevelopmental syndrome as a related phenotype) and Novel (no seizure phenotype described at all).

There is credible human genetic evidence linking RFX3 to infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, a form of epileptic encephalopathy: a single case report of IESS with ASD and an RFX3 mutation (PMID 37717291), a second reported case caused by a de novo 147 kb 9p24.2 microdeletion involving RFX3 (PMID 42653242), and RFX3 appearing among de novo CNV/sequence variant candidate genes in an IS/LGS exome cohort (PMID 26068938) and as a tier-2 cross-disorder DNM candidate including epileptic encephalopathy (PMID 33970367). However, the second case is a multigene microdeletion that cannot isolate RFX3, and the cohort findings are candidate-level rather than definitive, so only one bona fide single-gene proband report exists; the core established RFX3 phenotype remains ASD/ID/ADHD (PMID 33658631). Supporting biology (ciliary function, CREB-dependent activity-regulated neuronal gene expression; PMIDs 40060598, 25631876) makes the link plausible mechanistically but is not itself phenotype-level human evidence. This profile best fits "Existing," with modest weight on "Established" pending replication by additional single-nucleotide-variant probands.

FBN1 is firmly established as the Marfan syndrome/acromelic dysplasia gene (PMIDs 12203987, 30219651, 39741318, 29875127), with no connective-tissue mechanism linking it to epileptic encephalopathy. In the Taiwanese WES cohort (PMID 33333793), FBN1 was identified in the non-seizure group, explicitly not in epilepsy patients. The single infantile spasms case (PMID 41492575) attributes the DEE to a de novo CACNA1E variant and describes the FBN1 variant as an incidental, cardiovascularly relevant finding. The SUDEP review (PMID 40097380) lists FBN1 only as one of several candidate genes from a prior screen, a background citation rather than primary evidence, and SUDEP risk is not equivalent to epileptic encephalopathy. No article reports FBN1 variants causing epileptic encephalopathy in independent probands, so the co-mentions appear incidental.

The strongest evidence comes from PMID 35585091, which reports a single human patient with an EML1-like subcortical heterotopia phenotype (a malformation of cortical development strongly linked to epilepsy and intellectual disability) carrying a novel DLGAP4 variant, supported by extensive functional work (knockdown/overexpression, rescue failure with the mutant construct, heterozygous KO mice). This is one proband only, with no independent replication, so Established cannot be supported (no two human-variant papers with independent probands). The remaining DLGAP4 literature is animal/functional (SAPAP4-deficient mice with ASD-like behaviour, PMID 30664629), GWAS of anxiety (PMID 38328521), stroke circRNA polymorphism (PMID 34273101), or genomic-structure work (PMID 22510267), none addressing epileptic encephalopathy directly; PMID 26689812 concerns epilepsy but not DLGAP4. Points therefore split mainly between Existing (one human variant in an epilepsy-associated cortical malformation) and Hypothesized (strong but largely model-based biological plausibility).

The only neurodevelopmental article (PMID 27119313) reports a de novo 1q21.3 deletion in an ASD proband that happens to contain ANXA9 among 10 genes; the authors themselves attribute the phenotype to SETDB1 and explicitly state that the other genes, including ANXA9, are not known to relate to brain function. A multigene CNV cannot single out ANXA9, so this does not constitute gene-level evidence, and no second proband or point-variant study exists. All remaining articles concern ANXA9 in colorectal, gastric, and head/neck cancers or its biochemical Ca2+/lipid-binding properties, with no neural expression, pathway, or animal-model link. Therefore the co-mention is essentially incidental, favoring Novel, with a modest allowance for Existing because the gene does lie within a de novo pathogenic CNV found in an ASD patient.

Several human genetic studies implicate HLA-F regulatory variation in neurodevelopmental phenotypes: ASD-associated GWAS SNPs act as eQTLs regulating HLA-F in fetal cortex and immune tissue (PMID 34354167), and local genetic correlation/transcriptome analyses at chr6:29–30 Mb link HLA-F expression to ASD risk (PMID 38020478); a transdiagnostic TWAS also reports HLA-F among significant genes for schizophrenia (PMID 42448663). These are human, variant-based associations, but they are within the highly pleiotropic, strong-LD MHC region, making gene-level attribution uncertain and non-replicated at the level of a specific causal variant, so Established is not supported (no study reports HLA-F variants segregating in independent probands/families causing NDD). Supporting but non-genetic human data include dysregulated HLA-F expression in patient-derived hiPSC neurons (PMID 31358727) and MHC class I roles in synapse formation and neuron-glia signaling during cortical development (PMID 42158555), which keep a meaningful share on Hypothesized. Remaining papers (HLA-F structure, peptide presentation, transplantation, ALS, PTSD) are background immunology and do not address NDD.

Several human studies report de novo HDAC2 variants in probands with neurodevelopmental phenotypes: a de novo missense variant in a patient with a Cornelia de Lange-like phenotype (PMID 30806031), a de novo frameshift variant with functional characterization (mislocalization, altered acetylation, transcriptomic overlap with Rubinstein–Taybi) in a chromatinopathy patient (PMID 38753158), and a de novo probably pathogenic variant among candidate genes in a syndromic intellectual disability panel cohort (PMID 27620904). A large-scale statistical analysis of de novo SNVs/CNVs ranked HDAC2 as a top high-confidence novel NDD candidate gene (PMID 35468861), while 6q21q22.1 deletion reports (PMIDs 26052347, 38380230, 40847363) implicate HDAC2 only as part of multigene CNVs and cannot isolate it. Supporting biology (class I HDAC in chromatin remodeling complexes with ADNP, SMARCC2, MECP2, UBE3A pathways) further strengthens plausibility, but the clinical evidence remains a small number of single probands with heterogeneous phenotypes and no formal disease-gene validation, so Existing is slightly more likely than Established.

No article reports point variants in FAM222B causing a neurodevelopmental phenotype in independent probands. The 17q11.2 microdeletion case (PMID 27247625) only includes FAM222B among 43 genes in a multigene CNV and explicitly states that "little clue is available about the potential relationship of FAM222B ... with neurodevelopment," so it cannot single out the gene. The FAM222B disease associations reported elsewhere concern cerebral cavernous malformations (ultimately refuted, PMID 27587990) and cardiovascular laterality defects (PMID 42632841), neither of which is a neurodevelopmental disorder; the NMD-escape NDD trio study (PMID 38091987) does not implicate FAM222B. Some weak biological plausibility exists (interaction with tubulin cytoskeleton and STAMBP, linked to microcephaly-capillary malformation syndrome, and predicted haploinsufficiency), supporting a Hypothesized rather than Existing classification, with substantial probability that the co-mentions are purely incidental (Novel).

No article reports a point mutation or gene-specific variant in GPR27 in patients with neurodevelopmental disorder; the only human genetic data come from multi-gene 3p14.1/3p13 deletions (PMID 19332160, 39539796) that also remove FOXP1, PROK2 and EIF4E3, and the phenotype is attributed principally to FOXP1 — such contiguous CNVs cannot single out GPR27, so Established is excluded and even Existing is weak. Review and WES papers (PMIDs 22736078, 24083349, 29330474) merely restate this deletion as background, noting that a contribution from GPR27 "cannot be ruled out," which is speculation rather than evidence. Supportive biological plausibility exists: GPR27 is a brain-enriched super-conserved orphan GPCR (SREB) with synaptic partner interactions (PMID 37998360), altered expression in Shank3-overexpressing mice (PMID 30233305), and appearance as a male-biased fetal brain DEG in a prenatal estradiol model (PMID 41331623) — all non-human/functional data supporting Hypothesized. The remaining probability reflects the possibility that all co-mentions are incidental neighbouring-gene artefacts (Novel).

No article in this set reports patients with epileptic encephalopathy caused by CHD7 variants. CHD7's established human disease is CHARGE syndrome (PMIDs 20301296, 30384553, 29171162), and in the neonatal encephalopathy cohort (PMID 33775046) the CHD7 cases were classified as genetic syndrome, while the epileptic encephalopathy cases were attributable to KCNT1 and PACS2 — so CHD7 is a co-mention, not evidence. The main link to epileptic encephalopathy is indirect and biological: CHD2, a paralog in the same chromodomain helicase family, is a validated epileptic encephalopathy gene, and CHD7 is cited in those papers for shared helicase/chromatin-remodeling mechanism and CHD8 interaction (PMIDs 23708187, 33435571, 24207121). Additional neurodevelopmental/ASD and sleep-disturbance data for CHD7/CHD8/Kismet (PMID 34088660) and connectome/de novo variant analyses (PMIDs 32341405, 32522981) support neurodevelopmental relevance but not epileptic encephalopathy causation. This pattern best fits "Hypothesized," with residual probability for "Novel" since the co-mentions may simply be incidental.

Two large human de novo mutation studies implicate H2AC6 (HIST1H2AC) in NDD: Coe et al. (PMID 30559488) lists HIST1H2AC among genes with an excess of severe missense DNMs in developmental delay/autism cohorts, and Wang et al. (PMID 33004838) reports H2AC6 reaching FDR-level (not family-wise) significance for de novo missense enrichment across >17,000 NDD trios, noting it was initially selected as a CNV candidate gene. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence of association but falls short of replicated, clinically characterized probands with gene-level causal proof, and the cohorts substantially overlap. The RNU4-2 paper (PMID 38991538) merely cites H2AC6 as a previously NDD-associated gene (background citation, not new evidence), and the SMARCB1 and DNAJC6 papers mention H2AC6 only incidentally as a structural partner or differentially expressed histone. Therefore "Existing" is the most appropriate category, with some residual probability for "Established".

No article reports pathogenic single-gene GPS2 variants in patients with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The only human genomic evidence is a multigene 17p13.1 microdeletion in a boy with intellectual disability and epilepsy, in which GPS2 is merely one of ~17 candidate genes and the functional follow-up implicated GABARAP, not GPS2 (PMID 20111057); a contiguous deletion cannot single out GPS2. The remaining support is biological: GPS2 is an integral subunit of the NCoR/SMRT–HDAC3 corepressor complex, whose other components (HDAC3, TBL1XR1, ANKRD11, SETD5, MeCP2 recruitment) are established NDD genes, and GPS2 knockdown produces transcriptional changes correlated with ANKRD11/SETD5 loss (PMIDs 39047730, 42143056, 26769062, 32486848, 36835623, 40427580). GPS2 also interacts with the brain-specific transcription factor RFX4_v3 required for brain morphogenesis (PMID 18218630), and other papers concern cancer, inflammation or thrombocytopenia rather than NDD (PMIDs 22820256, 39791724). This pattern fits "Hypothesized" — strong pathway/biological relevance without patient-level variant evidence.

No article demonstrates that RAB14 variants cause neurodevelopmental disorder in independent probands; the closest human genetic data is the gene-family burden framework (PMID 32183904), which lists two de novo variants in RAB14 as part of a collectively enriched RAB2A/RAB4/RAB11/RAB14 family rather than gene-specific, exome-wide significant evidence. The CNV reports (PMIDs 37064343, 31277718, 42192297) include RAB14 (or its GEF DENND6B) only within multi-megabase deletions/duplications spanning dozens of genes, which cannot single out RAB14. Supporting biology is indirect: RAB14 interacts with VPS13B, the Cohen syndrome protein (PMID 35690661), and participates in endosomal/Golgi trafficking relevant to neurodevelopment (PMIDs 38565878, 25694446), and a murine ADHD model showed differential methylation at Rab14 (PMID 40465750, non-human). This supports a limited "Existing" claim at best, with substantial weight on hypothesized/biological plausibility and a real chance the co-mentions are incidental.

Two independent human genetic studies report their own primary patient data: PMID 41035394 identified six novel BRSK1 variants (mostly de novo SNVs/indels, with loss of protein) in seven probands with epilepsy/neurodevelopmental disorder, supported by a knockout mouse recapitulating seizures and behavioral deficits; PMID 42805187 independently identified ten individuals with rare heterozygous BRSK1 variants via the Texome Project and GeneMatcher, with Drosophila modeling showing partial loss-of-function. These are independent probands/cohorts, not CNVs, and both include functional corroboration, satisfying replication criteria for Established. Supporting biology (LKB1–SAD-A/SAD-B neuronal polarization pathway, PMIDs 17482548, 18339622) and the paralog BRSK2's established NDD association (PMID 30879638) strengthen plausibility. Some residual probability remains for Existing given the recency of both reports and limited independent clinical replication beyond them.

Two human genetic studies provide direct, variant-level evidence: the large-scale de novo variant analysis (PMID 35468861) lists KBTBD7 among candidates harboring recurrent damaging missense de novo variants in NDD probands, and the autism family sequencing study (PMID 38519481) reports a de novo missense variant (p.R617C) classified only as a VUS in an ASD proband. These are suggestive but not definitive—KBTBD7 did not reach the high-confidence candidate list, and the ASD variant remains a VUS, so replication with clear causal assertion is lacking. The 13q deletion study (PMID 34573300) includes KBTBD7 only within a 36-gene contiguous deletion region, which cannot implicate the gene individually. Remaining literature (lysophagy/NFKB signaling, cardiac inflammation, microglial septic brain injury in rodents, zebrafish rnf213a model) is non-human or in vitro but biologically relevant to neuroinflammation, supporting a hypothesized mechanistic contribution rather than human causal evidence.

Only one article (PMID 41290615) provides primary patient-level genetic evidence: two unrelated individuals with the same de novo heterozygous missense variant (p.Tyr654Ser) in MIDEAS causing a multisystem neurodevelopmental syndrome, supported by cryoEM structure and patient fibroblast expression data. Although this report includes two independent probands, it is a single publication without independent replication in a separate study, so the rule limits the rating to Existing at most. Supporting biological plausibility is strong: MiDAC regulates a neurodevelopmental gene expression program controlling neurite outgrowth (PMID 32297854) and intersects with MLL3/4 chromatin complexes (PMID 35820704), and HDAC1 complex assembly studies implicate MIDEAS structurally (PMID 40966515). The CMA autism study (PMID 37107578) and the Alzheimer methylation study (PMID 31217032) mention ELMSAN1 only incidentally in gene lists and do not implicate MIDEAS variants specifically. Hence Existing is most probable, with residual weight on Established given the two-proband de novo recurrence plus strong functional validation.

No article in this set reports de novo or inherited CBX5 (HP1α) point variants in patients with a neurodevelopmental disorder; the only clinical NDD gene with proven causal variants here is its paralog CBX1/HP1β (PMID 37087635), which cannot substitute for CBX5. The strongest "Existing"-leaning item is the 1p13.3 in silico CNV study (PMID 36277487), which lists CBX5 as a positional candidate within multigene microdeletions and cites ASD/DD cohort databases — a multigene CNV cannot single out CBX5, so this remains candidate-level. The bulk of evidence is mechanistic/biological: CBX5/HP1α is a core subunit of the ChAHP (CHD4–ADNP–HP1) complex mutated in Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome (PMIDs 36945042, 39808658, 42450350), a binding partner of POGZ in White–Sutton syndrome and of CHAMP1 in CHAMP1 syndrome (PMIDs 41499647, 39962076, 42748571), and is implicated in MeCP2/ATRX pericentric heterochromatin organization relevant to Rett and ATR-X syndromes (PMIDs 31671722, 22615490). This constitutes strong pathway/biology relevance without direct human variant evidence, making "Hypothesized" the best fit.

Human genetic evidence for ARID4A in neurodevelopmental phenotypes exists but is preliminary and non-replicated: a frameshift variant p.(Glu514ArgfsTer3) was reported as a candidate in one developmental language disorder family (PMID 39948625), a de novo missense (p.E564A) appears among candidate variants in an ASD exome cohort (PMID 39632905), a heterozygous missense (p.His411Asp) with functional DNA-binding characterization was reported in schizophrenia-affected siblings (PMID 35365808), and an intronic SNP in ARID4A showed ADHD-specific imaging–genetic association (PMID 40858546). None of these studies independently establishes causality at a Mendelian level; they are single-family or candidate-level findings across heterogeneous phenotypes, falling short of replicated clinical proof required for "Established." Supporting biology (epigenetic/imprinting regulation in mice, PMIDs 17043311, 35296332, 39369220; modifier of neurodegeneration in mouse models, PMID 29556029) is animal/in vitro and supports only a hypothesized mechanism. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing," with meaningful residual probability for "Hypothesized" if the human variants are discounted as candidates.

ot_trait: congenital disorder of glycosylation type II
justification: Multiple independent human studies report biallelic SLC39A8 variants causing a neurodevelopmental phenotype (intellectual disability, developmental delay, hypotonia, cerebellar atrophy, seizures) as SLC39A8-CDG. Boycott et al. (PMID 26637978) identified homozygous p.Gly38Arg in six Hutterite individuals and an unrelated Egyptian sibpair; Park/Riley-type follow-ups report additional probands with novel variants (PMID 32852845: homozygous p.F203S and p.G38R in two unrelated patients; PMID 34246313: two Italian siblings with novel variants plus a third unrelated patient), and further independent cases with treatment response (PMIDs 28749473, 41669571). Functional and mechanistic work (manganese deficiency, hypoglycosylation, mouse knock-in models) supports causality, and common variant rs13107325 additionally associates with neurodevelopmental outcomes in children (PMID 30619481). This constitutes replicated causal evidence in humans across independent families.

One recent human study (PMID 41408595) reports SEPTIN2 variants in five unrelated individuals and a mother–daughter duo, most with cognitive impairment, with supporting functional evidence of dominant-negative disruption of the axon initial segment and Ankyrin G binding. This is credible human genetic evidence, but it is a single report without independent replication, so "Established" cannot be assigned per the two-publication requirement. The 2q37 microdeletion reports (PMIDs 26238961, 36192675) include SEPT2 within multigene deletions and cannot single out this gene. Remaining literature (ZIKV protease cleavage of Septin-2, septin cytoskeletal biology, ciliogenesis, PANX1 interactome, growth cone transcriptomes) provides biological plausibility consistent with a "Hypothesized" link rather than variant-level evidence.

The strongest evidence comes from large-scale human de novo variant studies: PMID 35468861 lists KIAA0100 (BLTP2) among candidate NDD genes harboring recurrent damaging missense de novo mutations, PMID 32066658 prioritizes KIAA0100 among ASD candidate genes at 0.05 < FDR < 0.1, and PMID 31616000 reports a validated stop-gain de novo variant in KIAA0100 in a patient cohort table. These are statistical/candidate-level findings from cohort screens rather than clinically delineated, replicated patient series with functional confirmation, so causality is not established. No paper reports a defined KIAA0100-related syndrome in independent probands or families, which excludes the Established category. The Vps13-like/GPI anchor paper (PMID 35015055) concerns KIAA1109, not KIAA0100, and the THC paper is incidental, so neither supports the association.

No article in this list reports two or more independent human probands/families with single-gene PRKCE variants causing a neurodevelopmental phenotype, so Established cannot be supported. The rolandic epilepsy aCGH study (PMID 24372385) and other CMA studies (PMIDs 24297458, 36959829) implicate PRKCE only via multi-gene copy-number changes, which cannot isolate this gene. The strongest human-variant evidence is the de novo variant burden analysis in undiagnosed developmental disorder/autism cohorts, where PRKCE was prioritized among disease-associated nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes (PMID 37930872), plus a family-based endophenotype GWAS signal near PRKCE (PMID 36457050), supporting "Existing" at a limited level. The Prkce knockout mouse showing brain atrophy and cognitive/motor deficits as a model of SHORT syndrome (PMID 40914752) is compelling biology but is animal work, supporting Hypothesized; its reference to a single clinical PRKCE SHORT-syndrome case report is background rather than primary human evidence here.

The single provided article concerns CUL4B-based E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes, their phosphorylation-dependent recruitment of LIS1 and WDR1, and forebrain organoid development in the context of X-linked intellectual disability. It contains no data on ARPC4-TTLL3 (or the ARPC4/TTLL3 readthrough locus), no patient variants in this gene, and no functional link beyond a general mention of actin regulators. There is therefore no evidence—genetic or biological—connecting ARPC4-TTLL3 variation to neurodevelopmental disorder in this literature set. A small residual probability is allotted to "Hypothesized" because Arp2/3 complex subunits and tubulin tyrosine ligase-like proteins have general relevance to neuronal cytoskeletal development, but no such argument is made in the provided paper.

No article demonstrates a replicated causal link between GLYR1 point variants and neurodevelopmental disorder in independent probands, so Established is excluded. The strongest human genetic signal is a single de novo damaging coding variant in GLYR1 listed among 52 such genes in a primary complex motor stereotypies trio-sequencing study (PMID 37788244), which is suggestive but not gene-level significant; the CNV meta-analysis (PMID 38850022) only places GLYR1 within a multigene 16p13.3 interval alongside TSC2 and CREBBP and therefore cannot single it out. Biologically, GLYR1/NDF is a chromatin-associated factor regulating Pol II processivity (PMID 40430013) and is enriched at promoters of lncRNAs upregulated in cortical glutamatergic neurons (PMID 38913688), supporting a plausible but indirect mechanistic link, with additional rodent splicing data (PMID 42332800) being non-human. Its best-validated human disease associations are congenital heart disease (PMIDs 38070486, 42539127) and MSI colorectal cancer (PMID 32370786), not NDD, so weight is split between Existing and Hypothesized with meaningful residual probability for Novel.

Human genetic evidence exists but falls short of established causation: the OCD/chronic tic disorder whole-exome study (PMID 42680906) identified BRWD1 as a high-confidence large-effect risk gene with rare damaging/de novo variants and overlapping GWAS signal, and notes sharing of risk genes with other neurodevelopmental conditions; the TANC2 paper's supplementary data lists a validated de novo frameshift BRWD1 variant in an NDD/ASD cohort, but this is supportive table data rather than a dedicated clinical series. No two independent clinical reports delineate a BRWD1-specific NDD syndrome with point variants; the only Mendelian human phenotype proven (PMID 33389130) is asthenoteratozoospermia/PCD, not NDD. Remaining support is mechanistic or non-human: Brwd1 copy-number restoration rescuing cognition and LTP in Ts65Dn mice with upregulation in DS iPSC neurons (PMID 36289231), chromatin-remodeling/BAF biology, DS-region expression work (PMIDs 12889071, 12359327, 25052193), and multigene chr21 duplication/CNV reports (PMIDs 30619508, 38850022) that cannot isolate BRWD1. Thus "Existing" is most likely, with meaningful residual weight on "Hypothesized."

The great majority of the retrieved articles use γ-H2AX only as a generic biomarker of DNA double-strand breaks (PMIDs 18765297, 18772227, 24780228, 15279782, 38688170, 31267421, 33594057, 41123210), or report it as a downstream readout in models of other neurodevelopmental genes (MCM3, CECR2, MECP2) — these are citations of a marker, not evidence that H2AX variants cause disease. Functional/animal data (H2A.X knockout mESCs, Drosophila H2AV, Zscan5b) support only biological plausibility, consistent with "Hypothesized," since genome-stability/DDR failure is a recognized mechanism in microcephaly and intellectual disability syndromes. The only human genetic datum is a de novo H2AFX variant listed among 89 de novo genes in a Chinese ASD/ID trio cohort (PMID 36320054), with no functional follow-up or independent replication; this is suggestive but far short of established, and could support at most a weak "Existing." No article reports two or more independent probands/families with single-gene H2AX variants demonstrating causation, so Established is effectively excluded.

Nearly all listed articles use "NCL" as the acronym for neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN2/3/5/6/7/8, PPT1, MFSD8, TPP1) and are homonym hits unrelated to the nucleolin gene; these should be dismissed. The only relevant paper is PMID 35052391, which reports a single de novo frameshift indel (p.Gly664Glufs*70) in NCL (nucleolin) identified by whole-exome sequencing of an autism trio, supported by in vitro mislocalization and FRAP experiments, and notes that other de novo NCL variants have been reported in ASD/NDD cohorts. This is a single human proband with supporting functional work rather than replicated independent probands or families, so the evidence falls short of Established. Hypothesized retains some weight because much of the mechanistic support is cell-based (HEK293T transfection) rather than clinical genetic replication, while Novel is unlikely given a credible de novo variant in an affected individual.

No article reports independent probands or families with single-gene FBXL19 variants causing a neurodevelopmental disorder, so Established is excluded. The strongest human genetic signal comes from the CNV meta-analysis (PMID 38850022), which nominates FBXL19 as a candidate dosage-sensitive driver within 16p11.2/16p12.2 NDD-risk CNVs; however, multigenic CNVs cannot single out FBXL19, and it is only listed as a "possible" gene (not exome-wide significant) in the arachnoid cyst de novo variant study (PMID 36879130). Biological plausibility is substantial: FBXL19 is a CXXC-domain CpG-island reader that recruits the CDK-Mediator complex to prime developmental gene activation and interacts with MED13L, a bona fide NDD gene (PMID 40775066); it also regulates Rac3, implicated in neuronal development (PMIDs 31514269, 24684802), and belongs to the ubiquitin machinery expressed during corticogenesis (PMID 35974412). Most remaining literature concerns lung/endothelial inflammation and is irrelevant, and the GWAS mention of FBXL19 in suicidality failed replication (PMID 36515925), so the balance favors Hypothesized with meaningful probability for Existing.

The strongest evidence comes from PMID 41864309, which compiles 18 previously reported sporadic de novo SNVs in SUPT6H from individuals with developmental disorders, models them as likely loss-of-function, and supports this with Supt6 null/conditional knockout mice showing embryonic lethality, seizures, motor deficits and interneuron loss. However, that paper's own human component is a reanalysis of published variants rather than an independent clinical cohort with newly ascertained probands, and the mouse work is animal-based, so replication across independent clinical studies is not demonstrated. PMID 38850022 implicates SUPT6H as a dosage-sensitive driver within the 17q11.2 CNV locus, but a multigene CNV cannot single out this gene. The remaining papers describe SPT6/SUPT6H biology (RNAPII elongation, histone chaperone, chromatin regulation, differentiation) or incidental proteomic co-mentions, which support biological plausibility but not variant-level causation. Overall this fits "Existing" with meaningful residual weight on "Hypothesized."

Two primary human genetic reports describe pathogenic CAMK4 variants in patients: PMID 30262571 reports a de novo splice-disrupting gain-of-function variant (c.981+1G>A) in a proband with developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism and hyperkinetic movement disorder, with functional validation in proband-derived cells; PMID 33211350 reports a clustering of CAMK4 variants in independent individuals with a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring dystonia and chorea. These are independent probands with single-gene (not CNV) variants, supporting a causal role, and are corroborated by review/clinical literature (PMID 32657892, 39442785, 42817183). Supportive but weaker human association data exist for common CAMK4 variants in ASD/ADHD comorbidity (PMIDs 24442360, 31707462), while multigene 5q deletion reports (PMIDs 37510409, 39780213) cannot isolate CAMK4. Because the definitive monogenic evidence rests on a relatively small number of probands from two reports, some probability remains on "Existing".

Two independent primary reports identify patients with germline MAEA variants and neurodevelopmental phenotypes: PMID 41420108 describes eight patients with MAEA variants presenting a developmental delay/intellectual disability syndrome (DIADEM) with patient-derived cell line and mutation modeling evidence, and PMID 40880485 independently reports disease-linked missense variants (R34C, E349G, Y394D, M396R) in individuals with microcephaly, craniofacial, ocular and cardiac anomalies, with functional assays showing defective replication stress response. These are human single-gene variant studies, not CNVs, so they satisfy the replication requirement, though both are very recent and cohorts are small, leaving some chance of overlap or incomplete independence (hence substantial weight on Existing). Supporting mechanistic plausibility comes from the CTLH complex literature, where another subunit, WDR26, causes Skraban-Deardorff intellectual disability syndrome (PMID 38575527), and from MAEA's conserved role in this E3 ligase complex (PMID 24143168). Other listed papers (murine erythropoiesis, 4p16.3 contiguous deletions, general NDD reviews) do not add gene-specific human causal evidence.

Biallelic SLC18A3 variants are firmly established as a cause of presynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome in humans (PMID 27590285, 28188302, 33462016, 34943989, 31059209), and several of these primary reports describe neurodevelopmental features in independent probands: global developmental disability and learning difficulties (PMID 27590285), impaired motor and cognitive development with compound heterozygous missense/nonsense variants (PMID 34943989), and virtually absent developmental milestones in a homozygous p.Gly360Arg patient (PMID 28188302). SLC18A3 was also recovered as a diagnostic gene in a large exome-sequenced pediatric neurodevelopmental disorder cohort (PMID 37645600). However, the core, consistently replicated phenotype is a neuromuscular (CMS/fetal akinesia) disorder, and the developmental delay may in part be secondary to severe neonatal hypotonia, respiratory failure and prolonged ventilation, so the gene–NDD relationship is credible but not definitively established as a primary NDD gene. Other listed papers (deletion unmasking recessive alleles, reviews, expression/animal data) are background or non-gene-specific and do not add independent replication.

No article in this list reports a cohort or case series establishing SUMO2 variants as a cause of neurodevelopmental disorder; most SUMO2 papers are cell-biological (SUMOylation of DHX9, CENP-E, MEF2, TWIST2, APP, FIS1) and unrelated to NDD, with several being homonym-free but phenotype-irrelevant. The strongest human genetic hint is incidental: the AJAP1 study (PMID 38985877) lists a de novo nonsense variant, SUMO2 NM_006937.4 c.91C>T p.Gln31*, as an additional finding in a patient with epilepsy/NDD, which is a single, non-replicated, confounded observation. Supporting biological plausibility comes from SUMO2/3's documented role in neural stem cell proliferation/differentiation and synaptic function in ID (PMIDs 41507769, 32719102), from SUMO2-dependent regulation of the ID gene NACC1 (PMID 37533751), from ZMIZ1 network analysis (PMID 38686122), and from murine Sumo2 expression changes in a schizophrenia DOHaD model (PMID 42120553). This combination of mechanistic/animal data plus one incidental human de novo LoF variant places the weight mainly on Hypothesized with substantial probability for Existing, and essentially excludes Established since no two independent probands with SUMO2-attributed disease are reported.

No human genetic study reports SERPINA9 variants in probands with neurodevelopmental disorder. The only mechanistic mention (PMID 34355145) is a murine early-life penicillin/microbiome model in which Serpina9 appears as one of many differentially expressed transcripts in frontal cortex and amygdala; this is animal expression data, not human genetic evidence, and the gene is not functionally characterized as relevant to neurodevelopment. The ring chromosome 6 report (PMID 35248136) is irrelevant since SERPINA9 maps to 14q32.13, and in any case a multigene ring/CNV cannot implicate a single gene. Points are therefore split between Hypothesized (weak animal expression correlation in a neurodevelopmental paradigm) and Novel (the co-mention is essentially incidental, part of a large differential-expression list).

Two human genetic studies report ZNF483 variants in autism probands: a Chinese WGS trio study listing ZNF483 among 33 candidate risk genes with supporting expression/network evidence (PMID 39126614), and an Omani consanguineous cohort reporting a homozygous nonsense variant p.R683* (PMID 39769462). A GWAS of speech sound disorder also flags a locus near PTGR1;ZNF483 (PMID 34315907), adding suggestive but non-specific human support. These are candidate-gene discovery lists rather than replicated, well-powered clinical validation, so Established is unlikely; the microdeletion case (PMID 30847195) spans many genes and cannot implicate ZNF483 alone. Strong biological plausibility exists through ZNF483's interaction with MeCP2 and its role in neuronal differentiation, but that work is in vitro (P19 cells) and therefore supports Hypothesized rather than Existing (PMIDs 34192606, 31717404, 38027357).

No article reports PPP6R3 variants as a validated cause of neurodevelopmental disorder in independent probands or families, so Established is effectively excluded. The strongest human genetic hint is a de novo missense variant in PPP6R3 listed among 40 genes with DNVs in a small Chinese schizophrenia trio-exome study (PMID 26666178), where PPP6R3 was not among the prioritized genes, and inclusion of PPP6R3 within a large multigenic chromosome 11 duplication in an ADHD/ASD CNV pathway analysis (PMID 24954825), which cannot implicate the gene individually. Supporting biological plausibility comes from non-human and indirect work: a zebrafish ppp6r3 microexon mutant examined in an arousal/sleep study (where most microexon mutants showed mild or no phenotype, PMID 42319930) and PPP6R3 appearing as a predicted miR-135 target in a brain-disease review (PMID 39805813). The remaining papers concern PP6 holoenzyme biology in immunity, virology, glaucoma, and skeletal aging, which are incidental to neurodevelopment, leaving substantial probability on Hypothesized/Novel.

The only primary human genetic evidence specifically implicating PPFIA2 in neurodevelopmental disorder comes from a single report (PMID 41044885), which describes two unrelated individuals with de novo variants plus seven additional de novo variant carriers from large cohorts; this is credible but constitutes one publication rather than replicated independent clinical studies. The earlier Japanese SNP-array study (PMID 26740234) proposed PPFIA2 as a novel candidate ID gene, but it is based on copy-number variation, which cannot isolate PPFIA2 from neighbouring genes. Supporting biology is substantial (liprin-α2 as a presynaptic active zone scaffold, PMID 33761347; GIT1 interaction networks, PMID 35505090) and the paralogue PPFIA3 has an established syndromic NDD association (PMID 38181735), reinforcing plausibility but not replacing direct replication. Other listed papers (myopia, amblyopia, Slitrk review, Angelman model) mention PPFIA2 incidentally or in non-NDD phenotypes. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with some probability allocated to Established given the multi-proband de novo series.

No article in this set reports pathogenic RARA variants ascertained in patients with neurodevelopmental disorder; there is no paper with its own patient-level variant results, so Established is excluded. The strongest mechanistic support is biological: RARα directly interacts with FMRP and mediates synaptic retinoic acid signaling and homeostatic plasticity, whose loss underlies fragile X syndrome phenotypes (PMID 34205274), and RARA participates in retinoic-acid pathways implicated in developmental disorders (PMIDs 28612832, 21984809, 30578278) — all animal/in vitro work, hence Hypothesized. The only human genetic hint is an in silico candidate-gene review (PMID 36277487) that cites RARA as reported in an autism exome dataset, which is secondary citation rather than primary evidence, giving modest weight to Existing. Other listed papers (RAR = rest–activity rhythm, 9q21.13 deletion, HACE1, syndrome catalog) are homonyms or incidental co-mentions and do not contribute.

One primary clinical study (PMID 41033306) reports 14 individuals with de novo or loss-of-function EIF3B variants presenting with a syndrome including developmental delay, behavioral abnormalities, cardiac defects, and craniofacial dysmorphism, supported by zebrafish models of the orthologs. This is a single, albeit large and multi-center, report, so by the rule requiring at least two independent primary human genetic publications, the evidence falls short of Established. Supporting but non-decisive evidence includes 7p22.3 microdeletion cases (PMID 39152504) in which EIF3B is a candidate within a multigene deletion, which cannot isolate the gene, and review-level restatements (PMID 41708874). Remaining literature concerns eIF3b biochemistry in translation initiation, viral IRES function, and incidental proteomic co-mentions, which only provide biological plausibility.

No article reports multiple independent probands with pathogenic single-gene MAP3K12 variants, so Established is not supportable; the 12q13.13 microduplication/deletion report (PMID 28649281) spans ~20+ genes and cannot implicate MAP3K12 specifically. The strongest human genetic evidence is the de novo non-canonical splicing variant study (PMID 38113761), which identified MAP3K12 c.436G>A as a de novo variant in a patient with undiagnosed developmental disorder and experimentally validated aberrant splicing (exon 4 91-bp deletion), naming MAP3K12 a novel NDD candidate gene — a single, limited but credible human report consistent with "Existing." Substantial supporting biology exists but is largely non-human or degeneration-focused: DLK/MAP3K12 governs axon outgrowth, regeneration, synapse remodeling and presynaptic development via the RPM-1/Highwire pathway in C. elegans and mouse models (PMIDs 26051896, 24569480, 19652181, 39360902, 31805042), which would otherwise place the gene in "Hypothesized." Most remaining papers concern DLK inhibitors and neurodegeneration (Alzheimer's, ALS, injury), which are not neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Hence probability mass is concentrated on Existing with a sizeable residual on Hypothesized.

No article demonstrates a causal, replicated link between ZNF207 point variants and neurodevelopmental disorder; the 17q11.2 microdeletion reports (PMID 29130599, 37686382, 38596211) involve multigene CNVs where ZNF207 is only one of several haploinsufficient candidates and CDK5R1/RHOT1 are favoured, so they cannot establish causality. The strongest single-gene human evidence is the consanguineous Omani autism cohort (PMID 39769462), which reports a homozygous novel missense variant (p.G213R, classified likely pathogenic) in ZNF207 as a candidate ASD risk gene — a limited, non-replicated but credible human genetic observation supporting "Existing". The non-syndromic ID linkage study (PMID 36843831) only lists ZNF207 as one of ten positional candidates without identifying a variant, which is weaker and borders on hypothesis-generating. Additional biology (splicing regulation, transcriptional control, FMRP-related multi-omic analysis; PMIDs 41475346, 42266503, 36973293) provides mechanistic plausibility consistent with "Hypothesized". Overall, the evidence tips toward limited human association rather than established causation.

No article reports pathogenic ATF2 variants identified in human probands or families with a neurodevelopmental disorder; there is therefore no basis for "Established". The strongest evidence is biological/animal: ATF-2 knockout mice show ataxia, hyperactivity, reduced cerebellar Purkinje cells, enlarged ventricles and hearing loss (PMID 8538792), and ATF2 directly regulates Bdnf transcription alongside MYT1L and EGR1, factors tied to neurodevelopmental disease (PMID 39947922). Human data are indirect: ATF2 emerges as a hub gene in spatiotemporal brain co-expression modules enriched for psychiatric GWAS signal (PMID 33371872), and it appears in gene lists in Rett syndrome and enhancer/16p12.1 studies (PMIDs 39414258, 41279603) — these are network/co-mention level, not variant-level causal evidence, so a modest weight is given to "Existing". The remaining literature concerns chondrocyte, cancer and generic transcriptional biology, which does not support causality.

Multiple independent human clinical studies report pathogenic ANK3 variants in probands with neurodevelopmental phenotypes: PMID 38988293 describes 13 new individuals and reviews 27 total with mono- or biallelic ANK3 variants and detailed genotype–phenotype correlations; PMID 34218362 reports four additional individuals with heterozygous truncating variants; PMID 40879451 reports five individuals from three unrelated consanguineous families with homozygous pLOF variants and a recognizable ataxia-NDD phenotype; PMID 36777705 reports a homozygous missense variant in a consanguineous family; PMID 37263801 reports a de novo mosaic nonsense variant. These are independent probands/families with single-gene resolution (not CNVs), satisfying replication requirements. Functional work (PMID 31451636 on gAnkG neurodevelopmental missense mutations, PMID 31813652) provides supporting mechanism, further strengthening causality. Only a small residual probability is left for "Existing" given some phenotypic heterogeneity and VUS-level reports.

The strongest human genetic evidence is a single proband from an exome cohort (PMID 34946966) carrying a de novo frameshift in MSI1 (p.Arg199GlufsTer180) with microcephaly, intellectual disability and dysmorphism — though this patient also carried a second de novo variant in CBLC, weakening attribution. PMID 35977029 lists MSI1 among stress-granule-network genes with a nominal excess of de novo LGD variants across 40,853 NDD individuals, providing supportive but non-definitive human statistical evidence. The 12q24 deletion case (PMID 40018479) includes MSI1 among 122 deleted genes and cannot single out the gene, and PMID 42358771 only cites MSI1 as background. Substantial supporting biology exists (neural stem/progenitor expression, zebrafish CNS defects, C. elegans msi-1, tau splicing regulation), which would support Hypothesized if the human data were discounted. Because there is at least one credible human proband plus cohort-level de novo enrichment but no replicated independent families, "Existing" is the best fit.

No article reports pathogenic single-gene ING3 variants in patients with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The only human reports are multigene copy-number rearrangements (7q31.2-q33 duplication, PMID 22303804; t(7;22) duplication near ING3, PMID 23300646) where ING3 is merely speculated to contribute and cannot be isolated from neighboring genes, so they do not establish or firmly support an Existing classification. Strong biological plausibility exists: Ing3-null mice show embryonic lethality with failed neural tube closure and defective brain vesicle formation (PMID 31905726), C. elegans ing-3 mutants show an uncoordinated neuronal phenotype (PMID 19015549), and ING3 is a core H3K4me3-reader subunit of the TIP60/NuA4 complex whose catalytic subunit KAT5 causes a defined neurodevelopmental syndrome (PMIDs 32822602, 14966270, 40604793). Additional reviews propose ING proteins as epigenetic regulators of neural development (PMID 42196365). This pattern of animal-model, expression and pathway evidence without human variant data corresponds to Hypothesized.

Direct human genetic evidence exists: Pierce et al. (PMID 29386386) reported a de novo RING1 p.R95Q missense variant in a single girl with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder, supported by functional assays showing loss of H2A monoubiquitination and C. elegans modeling. A second primary study (PMID 41653922) reports identification of heterozygous mutations in RING1 (and RNF2) in individuals with NDDs, though its mechanistic results center on Rnf2/Ring1b mouse and cellular models. PMID 39256363 extends functional characterization of RING1 missense variants (hypomorphic effects on H2AK119ub and DNA damage repair in neural progenitors) but is largely in vitro and builds on the same patient allele. Other listed papers (PRC1 biology, limb development, Drosophila, CBX1, AUTS2, RNF2) cite RING1 as background or reflect paralog/complex biology rather than independent RING1 proband evidence. Because clearly documented, independent human probands are few (essentially one well-described case plus a newer cohort report), the evidence is best described as Existing, with meaningful probability that it now meets Established.

The primary human genetic evidence comes from a single large de novo variant study (PMID 35977029), which reported a nominally significant excess of de novo variants in core stress-granule genes including G3BP1 among 40,853 individuals with NDDs, with functional validation showing NDD-related variants disrupt the SG interaction network. This is one credible but not definitive human study; the gene-level signal was only nominal and the main established gene in that paper was UBAP2L (and CAPRIN1), not G3BP1. Secondary sources (PMIDs 39995077, 42401939, 34526993) list G3BP1 among NDD/ASD-associated RNA-binding proteins, but these restate the association as background rather than providing independent proband-level evidence, so replication criteria for "Established" are not met. Remaining weight goes to Hypothesized, since much supporting data is mechanistic/in vitro (G3BP1 as the central SG nucleator interacting with CAPRIN1, UBAP2L, DDX3X), providing strong biological plausibility without independent patient variant replication.

No article in this set reports LATS1 variants in human probands or families with neurodevelopmental disorder; LATS1 appears almost exclusively as a core Hippo pathway kinase in cancer, metabolic, and signaling studies (PMIDs 37937799, 34294713, 35613278, 27912098, 12379777). The only disease-variant evidence concerns WWC1 (W88C) in Tourette's syndrome, where LATS1/2 phosphorylation is a downstream readout in a mouse model, not a LATS1 variant (PMID 40153501). Reviews explicitly connect YAP/TAZ–LATS1/2 signaling to brain development and neurodevelopmental disorders, and mouse Lats1/Lats2 inactivation perturbs neural progenitor proliferation and survival (PMIDs 39936032, 41597251, 37124926), which supports biological plausibility rather than genetic causation. This pattern fits "Hypothesized": pathway and animal-model relevance without human variant data. A small residual probability is given to "Existing" in case unreported human association data exist, and some to "Novel" since several co-mentions are incidental.
