Human evidence exists at the single-gene level: a de novo nonsense variant (p.Tyr147Ter) in a patient with autism, intellectual disability, anxiety and obesity (PMID 27865048), a case report framed as "NLGN2-related neurodevelopmental disorder" (PMID 32405903), and a child with febrile/atypical absence seizures attributed to an NLGN2 variant (PMID 37506563); in addition, a large unified de novo SNV/CNV burden analysis of 41,165 NDD cases flagged NLGN2 as a high-confidence novel NDD gene (PMID 35468861), and rare missense variants with functional loss-of-function were reported in schizophrenia (PMID 21551456). These point toward more than a single isolated observation, supporting at least strong "Existing" and plausibly "Established" status. However, several of these are brief case reports without full detail, the 17p13.1 microduplication data (PMID 25123844) spans multiple genes and cannot implicate NLGN2 specifically, and much supporting work is mouse/in vitro (PMIDs 22820233, 38570872, 42737512, 33443230), which only supports "Hypothesized." Given the limited number of well-characterized independent probands with convincing single-gene causality, I weight "Existing" slightly above "Established."

The only direct human genetic evidence linking ATRN variants to a neurodevelopmental phenotype is a single consanguineous family in which two sibs with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy (developmental delay, hypotonia, spasticity, intellectual disability) carried a homozygous splice variant (PMID 28493104); this is one family, not independent replication, so Established cannot be supported. A second human report describes ATRN mutations and reduced expression in psychiatric (schizophrenia) subjects, but the mechanistic work is in zebrafish and the phenotype is not classic NDD (PMID 34869343). Remaining support is strong but non-human or functional: mouse mahogany and rat zitter/mv attractin mutants show CNS hypomyelination, vacuolation and neurodegeneration (PMIDs 11209055, 19931230, 17196964, 10086356), and in vitro neurite assays (PMID 12230323). Several cited CNV/array papers only include ATRN within multigene 20p13 deletions/duplications or mention it incidentally, which cannot single out the gene. Hence Existing is most probable, with substantial residual weight on Hypothesized given the predominance of animal data.

The strongest direct human evidence is the large-scale targeted sequencing study (PMID 33004838), which reports CASZ1 among genes reaching family-wise error rate significance for de novo mutation excess in >17,000 NDD trios — a credible but single primary dataset. Additional support comes from a CNV meta-analysis identifying CASZ1 as a dosage-sensitive driver candidate within 1p36 NDD-risk loci (PMID 38850022), but multigene deletions (also PMIDs 26345236, 41556146) cannot isolate CASZ1 from neighbors such as RERE, KCNAB2, or SKI, so they do not count as replication. Most other CASZ1 literature concerns cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, varicose veins, or neuroblastoma (PMIDs 28099117, 36293425, 23892435, 25953344), which are not neurodevelopmental phenotypes, and one Alzheimer's biomarker study reports a non-mediating association with a synaptic marker (PMID 35173266). Because I cannot cite two independent primary studies reporting single-gene CASZ1 variants in NDD probands, the evidence falls short of Established and best fits Existing, with some residual probability for Established given the robustness of the de novo burden signal.

PMID 40819229 reports 22 individuals with de novo XPO1 single-nucleotide/in-frame variants (half loss-of-function) sharing an overlapping phenotype, with Drosophila knockdown supporting developmental and habituation defects—this is a dedicated clinical cohort of many independent probands establishing a dominant monogenic NDD. Independently, PMID 35468861 found statistically significant enrichment of de novo deleterious variants in XPO1 across 41,165 NDD cases and ranked it a high-confidence NDD gene, providing human genetic support from a separate dataset. Additional support is indirect: 2p15p16.1 microdeletion/microduplication reports (PMIDs 39050773, 36807877, 42315110, 29951117, 38392344) implicate XPO1 as a candidate, but contiguous CNVs cannot isolate XPO1 from USP34/BCL11A and therefore do not count as gene-specific evidence. Other XPO1 papers concern nuclear export biology, ALS/TDP-43, or cancer and are mechanistic or homonymous (CRM1) co-mentions. Given one large definitive proband cohort plus a corroborating statistical de novo study, Established is most likely, with residual probability on Existing because formal independent replication rests largely on a single primary report.

MAZ lies within the recurrent 16p11.2 CNV region strongly associated with NDDs, but multigene CNV reports (PMIDs 39202413, 36320065, 38850022, 41155467, 42513527) cannot isolate MAZ from neighbouring genes and therefore do not constitute gene-level causal evidence. The strongest single-gene human data are a WES reanalysis of recessive intellectual disability that identified MAZ as a novel candidate gene supported by segregation in one family (PMID 39748273), and intragenic loss-of-function MAZ variants reported in colobomatous microphthalmia, a developmental phenotype in families where 16p11.2 deletions also carry neurodevelopmental features (PMIDs 41339071, 32571845 – the latter chiefly ocular and mouse-based). Mechanistic work places MAZ as a 16p11.2-encoded transcription factor repressing histone H1 genes with downstream dysregulation of ASD-associated gene networks (PMID 42169156), which is strong biological plausibility rather than variant-level proof. Because only a single credible human genetic report ties intragenic MAZ variation to an NDD phenotype, without independent replication in additional probands, the evidence falls short of Established and best fits Existing, with substantial residual weight on Hypothesized given the reliance on functional/animal data.

ot_trait: mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 13
justification: Most of the provided articles use "IK" as a homonym acronym for the intermediate-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ channel (KCNN4/KCa3.1) and must be dismissed (PMIDs 35715699, 36503451, 39637180, 2002364, 30973325), as must the NDD papers that concern entirely different genes (FBXW7, HUWE1, TMX2, ZNF711/SRCAP, RNU2-2) and never implicate the IK gene. The only item referencing the actual IK gene is a human eQTL-based Mendelian randomization/SMR and colocalization study that listed IK among six druggable genes significantly associated with schizophrenia (PMID 40685484) — a neurodevelopment-related psychiatric phenotype, but this is expression-level association rather than patient variant evidence, and it is a single, non-replicated statistical study whose focus is FGFR1. No article here reports pathogenic IK variants in independent probands or families, so Established cannot be supported. The balance therefore sits between Existing (one limited human association with a neurodevelopmentally linked disorder) and Novel (if schizophrenia MR evidence is deemed insufficient/incidental), with some weight for Hypothesized given no direct mechanistic brain-biology data for IK is presented.
